What can be more mobile and subtle than wisdom, which created all things, governs all things, arranges all things, directs all things? For in it we live, move, and have our being. Moreover, it reaches everywhere because of its purity, for it is light, and there is no darkness at all in it.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It is evident that the only-begotten Son of God, born from the substance of God the Father, is coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father, and therefore nothing impure is found in him, because no evil approaches the highest good, but the simple good always remains the same.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 1.7.48-49

The apostle says that Christ is the image of the Father. He says in fact that he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creatures. He speaks of the firstborn, and not of the first created, so that we would believe that by nature he is generated, and first from all eternity. Elsewhere the apostle says, "He made him heir of all things, and through him he also made the world, the one who is the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his being." The apostle says that he is an image, and Arius says that he is different. Why, then, speak of an image, if he were not the same? People ordinarily do not accept the image of a portrait as being different from the original, but Arius asserts that the Father is different from the Son. He maintains that the Father generated someone who is different from him, as though he were incapable of generating someone like himself. The prophets say, "In your light we see light." They say, "He is a reflection of the eternal light, an unspotted mirror of the majesty of God and an image of his goodness." See in how many ways they speak. "Radiance," because the brightness of the Father's light is in the Son. "Unspotted mirror," since the Father is visible in the Son. "Image of his goodness," since it is not one body seen reflected in another but the whole power of the Godhead in the Son. "Image" teaches that here is no difference. "Imprint" indicates that he is the manifestation of the Father. "Splendor" bespeaks eternity. In fact, the "image" is not the bodily face, nor is it made with colors or from wax but is simply from God. He is from the Father, pouring forth from the spring.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke, PL 1786C

Therefore the Son is good, for He is the Radiance of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God's majesty, and the image of His goodness (Wis. 7:26). How then is He not good, who is the image of goodness? For just as the image of God is God, but there is one God, so also the image of divine goodness is good, but there is one goodness. Certainly, it is useful for me to believe that God is good, since He will be the judge of my sins. Let those who do not wish to believe that He is good see to themselves. And so, because this man who is testing is a lawyer, as is shown in another book, he spoke well: No one is good except God (Mark 10:18); so that he might be reminded that it is written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Deut. 6:16), but rather confess to the Lord, For He is good (Ps. 135:1). (Verse 21.) Finally, He often rebukes him, for he boasted in the law that he had kept all things from his youth; in order to expose his empty boasting, He shows him that he still lacks what is of the Law. And so he is brought to sadness by the command of mercy, so that a certain natural form of judgment might be given against him.
ON THE TRINITY 4:20.27

What wonder, therefore, if He is sent, not because He is unequal with the Father, but because He is "a pure emanation issuing from the glory of the Almighty God?" For there, that which issues, and that from which it issues, is of one and the same substance. For it does not issue as water issues from an aperture of earth or of stone, but as light issues from light. For the words, "For she is the brightness of the everlasting light," what else are they than, she is light of everlasting light? For what is the brightness of light, except light itself? and so co-eternal with the light, from which the light is. But it is preferable to say, "the brightness of light," rather than "the light of light;" lest that which issues should be thought to be darker than that from which it issues. For when one hears of the brightness of light as being light itself, it is more easy to believe that the former shines by means of the latter, than that the latter shines less. But because there was no need of warning men not to think that light to be less, which begat the other (for no heretic ever dared say this, neither is it to be believed that any one will dare to do so), Scripture meets that other thought, whereby that light which issues might seem darker than that from which it issues; and it has removed this surmise by saying, "It is the brightness of that light," namely, of eternal light, and so shows it to be equal. For if it were less, then it would be its darkness, not its brightness; but if it were greater, then it could not issue from it, for it could not surpass that from which it is educed.
TRACTATES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 20:13

See God, see His Word inhering to the Word speaking, that the speaker speaks not by syllables, but this his speaking is a shining out in the brightness of wisdom. What is said of the Wisdom itself? "It is the radiance of eternal light." Observe the radiance of the sun. The sun is in the heaven, and spreads out its brightness over all lands and over all seas, and it is simply a corporal light. If, indeed, thou canst separate the brightness from the sun, then separate the Word from the Father. I am speaking of the sun. One small, slender flame of a lamp, which can be extinguished by one breath, spreads its light over all that lies near it: thou seest the light generated by the flame spread out; thou seest its emission, but not a separation. Understand, then, beloved brethren, that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are inseparably united in themselves; that this Trinity is one God; that all the works of the one God are the works of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The Apostle says of the same Son: Who, being the brightness of glory, and the express image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power (Heb. 1:3). For the Father calls him Wisdom itself so that he is his Word, not as a word is uttered from the mouth with sound, or thought before it is spoken; for this is accomplished within the spans of time, but that is eternal, and by enlightening he tells us both about himself and about the Father, what must be said to men, and therefore he says: No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matt. 11:27). Because the Father reveals through the Son, that is, through his Word. For if this word which we utter is temporal and transitory, and shows itself and that about which we speak; how much more does the Word of God, through whom all things were made, show the Father as he is, because it too is as he is, and this is what the Father is, according to wisdom and essence. For according to the Word, he is not what the Father is, because the Word is not the Father; and the Word is spoken of relatively, as the Son, who certainly is not the Father; and therefore Christ is the power and wisdom of God, because from the Father as power and wisdom, he too is power and wisdom, as the light of God and from the Father as light, and the fountain of life with God the Father, who is surely the fountain of life: For with you, he says, is the fountain of life. In your light we shall see light (Ps. 36:9); because as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself (Jn. 5:26). And he was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world; and this light was the Word with God, but the Word was also God. Now God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. But the light is not bodily but spiritual; nor is it so spiritual that it is made by illumination, as was said to the apostles: You are the light of the world; but the light which enlightens every man, that very highest wisdom is God, of whom we are now speaking. Therefore the Son is Wisdom, from the Father who is Wisdom: as light from light, and God from God, so that both the Father is light, and the Son is light, and the Father is God, and the Son is God. Therefore both the Father is wisdom, and the Son is wisdom, and therefore both together are one light, and one God, therefore both one wisdom, but the Son was made wisdom for us from God, and righteousness and sanctification, because we turn to him temporally, and that from a certain time, so that we may remain with him forever, and he too from a certain time the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
ON THE CHRISTIAN FAITH 4.143-44

"O the depths of the riches, the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How inscrutable his judgments and unsearchable his ways! In fact, who has ever known the thoughts of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has given him something, so as to receive something in return? Since from him, because of him and for him all things are. To him be glory forever." Of whom does this speak—the Father or the Son? Perhaps of the Father? But the Father is not the Wisdom of God, because the Wisdom of God is the Son. And what can Wisdom not do, of whom it is written, "Though one, she can do all things; though remaining in herself, she renews all things"? Thus we read that Wisdom is not something temporary but permanent. According to Solomon, then, Wisdom is all-powerful and permanent. You will also read that it is good, because it is written, "Against wisdom, wickedness cannot prevail."
Confessions 7.11.17

Observing, then, all the other things put beneath you, I discovered that they neither wholly exist, nor do they wholly not exist. They exist, since they are from you, but they also do not exist because they are not what you are. For only what exists immutably, truly exists. It is good for me to be in union with God then, since, if I do not remain in him, neither can I remain in myself. He, by contrast, "remaining stable in himself, renews all things." "You are my Lord, because you have no need of my goodness."
SERMON 212:1

You believe in God, the Father almighty, invisible, immortal, king of the ages, creator of all things visible and invisible, and so on according to what is said of him, either by right reason or by the authority of sacred Scripture. From this greatness of the Father, then, you must not exclude the Son. Because these are things that are not said exclusively of the Father, as though he were unrelated to the one who said, "I and the Father are one," and of whom the apostle said, "Who, being divine in nature, did not consider robbery his equality with God." Robbery is the usurping of something that belongs to another, but this equality is his by nature. Consequently, how is the Son not almighty, through whom all things were made, who is also the power and the wisdom of God, that wisdom about which it is written, "Being one, she can do all things"? That nature is therefore also invisible, by the very fact that he is equal to the Father.
City of God 11.4.1

The world is the greatest of the visible beings. God is the greatest of the invisible beings. But we see that the world exists, and we believe that God exists. No one makes us believe with more certainty that God created the world than God himself. And when did we hear this? Nowhere better than in the holy Scriptures, where his prophet said, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." Was this prophet perhaps present when God created the heavens and the earth? No. But the Wisdom of God was there, through whom all things were made. Entering holy souls, this Wisdom makes friends of God and prophets, silently making her works known in them. With them the angels of God also speak, who always see the face of the Father, and communicate his will to those to whom it must be communicated. And one of these was this prophet who said and wrote, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." And this is a text so trustworthy for belief in God that, thanks to the same Spirit of God through whom he knew these revealed things, he also predicted, long ago, the advent of our faith.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, when something is pronounced or narrated in the Scriptures about wisdom, whether by wisdom itself speaking, or when something is said about it, the Son is especially indicated to us, by the example of whose image we also may not depart from God, because we too are the image of God, not indeed equal, for we are made by the Father through the Son, not born of the Father as that wisdom is; and we, because we are illuminated by the light, but that wisdom truly because it is the light illuminating, and therefore that wisdom is without an example, but for us it is an example. For it does not imitate anyone preceding it to the Father, from whom it is never separable, because it is the very same as He from whom it is; but we, imitating, imitate the one who remains, and we follow the one who stands, and walking in Him we strive toward Him: because He became for us a temporal way through humility, who is for us an eternal dwelling through divinity; for indeed, to pure intellectual spirits who have not fallen by pride, in the form of God and equal to God, and God, He offers the example, so that the same example might also offer a way of return to fallen man, who, because of the uncleanness of sins and the punishment of mortality, could not see God, He emptied Himself, not by changing His divinity, but by assuming our changeableness, and taking the form of a servant, He came to us in this world, who was in this world, because the world was made through Him, so that He might be an example above for those seeing God, an example below for those marveling at man, an example for the healthy to remain, an example for the weak to recover, an example for the dying not to fear, an example for the dead to rise again. In all things He Himself holds the primacy, for man ought not to follow anyone but God to attain happiness, and he could not perceive God by following, so he would follow God made man, at once both the one whom he could perceive and the one whom he ought to follow. Indeed, the Almighty Father begot almighty wisdom from Himself, which, remaining, renews all things in itself, because it, being absolute, rules and orders all changeable things by its will, which, transferring itself into the souls of the elect, by its grace makes them friends of God, and appoints them prophets. For all things were made through Him, and without Him was made nothing (Jn. 1:3). Therefore it is said: You have made all things in wisdom, because through His Son, that is, His Word and His wisdom, God made all things. (Prov. 3:9)
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

If God loves no one except him who dwells with wisdom, then surely He hates all followers of foolishness. Therefore, it is declared in this statement that anyone who hates discipline cannot be a partaker of the grace of God, because the Lord is far from the wicked, and he who hates rebuke will die (Prov. 15:29). Therefore, the heart of the wise seeks doctrine, and the mind of the just will meditate on obedience. But he who trusts in his own heart is foolish; and he who walks wisely, this one will be saved (Prov. 15:10).
On the Duties of the Clergy 2.13.64

Who would ever ruin the loveliness of a beautiful face by joining it with a beast-like body and claws? Indeed, the appearance of virtue is admirable and splendid, and especially the beauty of wisdom, as the succession of events narrated by Scripture demonstrates. Wisdom is more dazzling than the sun, and, compared with the light of the constellations, it surpasses them all. Indeed, whereas the night absorbs their light, wickedness cannot overcome wisdom.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

According to history, wisdom is said to be more splendid than the sun and the brightness of all the stars: for bodily light, which, being changed by the alternation of day and night, sometimes appears and sometimes is hidden, when compared to the spiritual and perpetual light of wisdom, seems to have scarcely the small brilliance of a certain spark. For every temporary thing, when compared to what is everlasting, seems as if it no longer exists, since it is consumed by eternity. Therefore, in a mystical sense, the brightness of the wisdom of God, which is Christ, when compared to the splendor of any of the saints, whom He here calls by the name of the sun and stars, far surpasses them, because they are changeable, but He always remains the same. The Psalmist, contemplating this, says to the Lord Himself: In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; all of them will grow old like a garment, and like clothing you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will have no end (Ps. 102:25-27).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Since none of the elect in this life is immune from sin; therefore, no wickedness approaches Christ. Of whom it is written: Blessed is the just man in the Lord who has been found without stain (Sir. 31). And again: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth (Isa. 53:9). To whom the prince of this world comes and finds nothing in him. Nevertheless, he himself bore our weaknesses and carried our diseases, because he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness; by whose wounds we have been healed (1 Peter 2:24).

n: She. The uncreated wisdom is infinite; and the created is the most excellent of God's gifts. (Worthington) --- Sweetly. God is every where present, (St. Bernard) and directeth all with ease. (St. Augustine, ep. ad Dard. q. i.)

Works. Directing us to imitate them, as much as possible. (Haydock) --- She teaches us how to refer all to God, (Menochius) while mere philosophers stop at vain speculations, and barren admiration of the Deity.
Are. Wisdom is an universal teacher. But she particularly inculcates virtue. All science which has not this tendency is vain. (Calmet)

Speeches. Rhetoric, (Grotius) or doubtful matters, as Solomon discovered the real mother, 3 Kings iii. 27. --- Arguments. Greek, "riddles," which were much in fashion, 3 Kings x. 1. (Calmet) --- Wonders. Such as comets and eclipses. (Menochius) --- When Anaxagoras discovered the latter, he durst not write, but only instructed his disciples in secret, for fear of being taken for an atheist, or magician. (Plut.[Plutarch?] in Nicias.) --- The sciences, which are now common, were formerly confined to few; and the people looked upon eclipses as so many prodigies. The wise man is possessed of all natural sciences, and can predict the changes of weather, &c. --- Ages. Forming a judgment of futurity from past occurrences.

After me. He speaks to the great, who are more sensible of glory. Solomon's fame would have continued untarnished, if he had not fallen, (Calmet) and we may hope that he repented, and verified this prediction. (Haydock) --- It is not certain that he obtained immortal glory. (Worthington)
Of me. Wisdom is the best protection. --- Good and valiant. These are the two most essential qualifications of kings.
Received. "By lot," sortitus, (Haydock) to exclude all preceding merit. (St. Augustine, de Gen. lit. x. 18.) --- Good soul. Natural dispositions (Pineda) are perfected by grace and labour. (Calmet)

More good. The pre-existence of souls seems to be insinuated, though this is not clear, and the opinion is now rejected. Some are born with a better disposition for learning than others. (St. Augustine, contra Jul. iv. 3.) --- Yet none possess any seeds of virtue by nature, or are more infected than others, with original sin, as some heretics would assert. (Calmet)

Continent. All good must come from God. (Haydock) --- Chastity cannot be preserved without his aid. (St. Augustine, Confessions vi. 11.) --- Yet this seems not to be the literal sense. Solomon prays for the acquisition of wisdom, (Calmet; Ecclesiasticus vi. 28., and xv. 1.; Menochius) which includes continence, religion, and every virtue. (Haydock)

f: Against Marivadus the Arian, PL 62

On common renewal. The Father renews, the Son renews, and the Holy Spirit does this. Of the Father in Jeremiah: Convert us, O God, and we shall be converted to you: renew our days as from the beginning (Lam. 5:21). Of the Son in Solomon: For it reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1), and, Being one, it makes all things new (Wis. 7:17). Of the Holy Spirit to the Romans: But now we have been discharged from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter (Rom. 7:6).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, the only-begotten Son of God is co-eternal and co-equal in all things to the Father and to the Holy Spirit. From end to end, that is, from eternity to eternity, he reaches mightily, because he is the power of God; and he arranges all things sweetly, because he himself is wisdom, who in the Revelation of John therefore says: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God (Rev. 22:13). The beginning, whom no one precedes. The end, to whom no one succeeds in the kingdom, who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty. Who elsewhere through the Prophet says: Before me no god was formed, and after me there will not be (Isa. 43:10). Otherwise, wisdom reaches from end to end mightily when, from the beginning of the creation of the world to the coming of the Lord, it mightily asserts the wondrous works of God and the pure testimonies of the divine law through the Old Testament, and from the incarnation of the Word to the end of the world, it sweetly explains the sweetness of the divine commandments through the Gospel. Therefore, the one and the same creator is of both Testaments, namely the mediator of God and men, who in the law commended the fear of himself to his elect, and in the Gospel the love of himself. Therefore, elegantly, wisdom is said to reach from end to end mightily: because everywhere it is proclaimed to be of flawless and perfect virtue; for we often find in the Scriptures that the end is put for perfection, as is that saying of the Apostle: The end of the commandment is charity, from a pure heart and a good conscience, and faith sincere (1 Tim. 1:5). And again: The end of the law is Christ for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10:4). Therefore also in the Gospel, Truth itself wished to show that the two precepts of love are the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets, and answered the lawyer, saying: On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:40), that is, all the doctrine of the Law and the Prophets is fulfilled in these, and in these is completed.
HOMILIES ON GENESIS 6.1

I think, therefore, that Sarah, who is interpreted 'princess' or 'one exercising rule', holds the figure of ἀρετή, which is the virtue of the soul. This virtue, then, is joined and cleaves to a wise and faithful man, just as also that wise man who said concerning wisdom: "I sought to bring her to me as my bride." Therefore for this reason it is said by God to Abraham: "in all things whatsoever Sarah shall say to you, hearken to her voice."
COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

you will find that divine Scripture has shunned the word "love" (amor) and has put "charity" and "affection" (dilectio) instead. Sometimes, though rarely, it does name love by its proper word, and it invites and incites souls toward it, as when it says in Proverbs concerning wisdom: "Love her, and she will keep you; surround her, and she will exalt you; honor her, and she will embrace you." But also in that little book which is called the Wisdom of Solomon, it is written thus concerning wisdom itself: "I became a lover of her beauty." … For if it had said that Isaac fell in love with Rebecca, or Jacob with Rachel … But most plainly, in this very little book which is now in hand, the name of love has been exchanged for the word "charity," in the place where it says: "I have adjured you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my kinsman, that you tell him that I am wounded with charity" … Therefore it makes no difference in the divine Scriptures whether it be called charity, or love, or affection, except that the name of charity is exalted to such a degree that even God himself is called charity, as John said: "Beloved, let us love one another, for charity is of God, and everyone who loves is born of God, and knows God; but he who does not love does not know God, for God is charity."
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

I have loved her, I have sought her from my youth. The lover of wisdom says that he has sought wisdom itself from his youth, that is, from the cradle of human life, and therefore he has truly found it, because he was a diligent seeker of it, according to that promise which she elsewhere made to her lovers, saying: Blessed is the man who listens to me, and who watches at my doors daily, and observes the posts of my gates (Prov. 8:34). Whoever finds me finds life, and will draw salvation from the Lord (Prov. 8:35). And again: I, she says, love those who love me, and those who watch for me in the morning will find me (Prov. 8:17). And I sought to take wisdom as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty. I sought, he says, to take wisdom as my bride, that is, to join her to myself in a perpetual covenant, from whose companionship I know that I never wish to be separated, and whose beauty I have chosen to desire above all; for the beauty of wisdom is truth, which all who are truly religious especially long to know: because it is by this alone that all the elect of God hope to be made blessed in eternal rest. Therefore, Truth itself says to the Father in the Gospel: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (Jn. 17:3).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Generosity is glorified by having fellowship with God. Therefore, generosity and nobility belong to the only-begotten Son, to have an eternal and omnipotent Father, with whom he himself remains coequal and coeternal from the beginning: because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (Jn. 1:1-2). The Lord of all sits and loved her. Because the Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand: For she is the teacher of God's discipline, and the chooser of his works. John clearly proves this in the Gospel, saying: He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was before me, and from his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace: because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has seen God at any time. The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him (Jn. 1:15-18).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

And if riches are sought in life, what is richer than wisdom, which accomplishes all things? Therefore, the wisdom and power of God is the Lord Christ, through whom all things were made, and who, together with the Father, arranges and governs all things by his own will, according to the saying of the Gospel: My Father, he says, works even now, and I work (Jn. 5:17). He contains within himself the riches of all virtues, and distributes them to his lovers according to his will, as is equally declared in both the New and the Old Testament. Therefore, as wisdom itself speaks in Proverbs, saying: With me are riches and glory, lofty sheep and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce than chosen silver. I walk in the ways of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of judgment, that I may enrich those who love me, and fill their treasures (Prov. 8:18–21). So also in the Gospel, the same cries out and says: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (Jn. 8:12). Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matt. 11:28-30). And elsewhere: Everyone, he says, who has left house or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will possess eternal life (Matt. 19:29). This saying can also especially pertain to those who meditate on the divine law, who meditate on it day and night properly, and are constant in contemplation, because whoever seeks it with attentive heart and good determination will be filled with the indescribable sweetness of its inner truth, and will enjoy the abundance of all good things.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

But if sense is at work, which of these is more an artificer than that? If, therefore, wisdom is the creator of sound sense and profound understanding, how is it that she herself is not the producer of all good works, of sacred virtues, which offer lasting salvation to their lovers?
On the Duties of the Clergy 2.13.65

Wisdom does not live with vice in any way but unites without conflict with the other virtues. Her spirit is intelligent, without blemish, trustworthy, holy, loving of the good, acute, not opposed to any good, beneficent, stable, sure, possessing all virtues and seeing all. And then, "She teaches temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude."
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

And if anyone loves justice, the labors of it possess great virtues. No one can attain the prize of righteousness unless he follows the rule of wisdom, because it preserves the standard of equity and leads by the way of truth to eternal life. For indeed, the labors of it possess great virtues, because there is nothing idle, nothing combative in its works, but whatever things are true, whatever are pure, whatever are righteous, whatever are holy, whatever are lovable, whatever are of good reputation, these it performs; and it entrusts these things to its lovers to be done, so that by the practice of this good they may obtain eternal life; for the fruit of light is in all goodness, and righteousness, and truth. for she teaches soberness and caution, righteousness and courage, than which nothing is more useful in life for human beings. Not only do philosophers believe that there are four principal virtues, but our own authorities also agree, which here are called restraint, wisdom, righteousness, and virtue. Elsewhere, however, these same virtues are called by different names: wisdom, righteousness, courage, and restraint. But what these four are, or what the works of each are, we ought briefly to demonstrate with the Lord enlightening us. Hardly anyone is ignorant that the number four is sacred to perfection, since the whole world is found to be bounded by four parts or corners: east, west, north, and south; and Adam himself, the father of the human race, or the general name which is called "man," is spelled with four letters. The body also, constructed from four elements, contains within itself the mystery of the number four. Even the soul itself is said to have four affections, by which we are led either to good or to evil; and the ancients discovered this subtly, and their discoveries have been approved and received by their successors. Moreover, the four rivers which flow from the source of paradise, or the four Gospels as the divine course of the wheel, and the four living creatures, their four wings and faces, all abundantly commend the dignity of this number. Therefore, we must carefully consider how much perfection these virtues, which are so numerous, contain in their number, how much sanctity they grant upon the Christian soul, and how there is nothing perfect anywhere which is not found in these virtues. For if restraint makes one moderate, wisdom wise, righteousness righteous, and courage brave, I do not know what could be more perfect than one who acts with restraint, righteously, wisely, and bravely. Therefore, it is indeed difficult for us to show the names of the individual virtues from which perhaps other virtues arise, which originate from those four we have called principal; but when their properties and actions begin to be revealed, it may appear from the effects what virtues arise from each. Nevertheless, above all, we must know and hold that these four virtues, or all those which arise from them, are gifts of God, and that no one has, had, or will have them except to whom God, who is the source and origin of all virtues, has granted them. For whoever at any time, in any nation, believed in God and lived by faith, could certainly become moderate, wise, righteous, or brave by His gift. But those who, not knowing God or even blaspheming, lived without faith, are to be believed to have been unable to receive or possess any of those virtues from God. For all have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one (Ps. 14:3). And although they seemed to have a certain appearance of holiness, they were entirely ignorant of its power, because they were unwilling to submit to their Creator. Therefore, searching various things and striving by different inquiries and debates, they did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they find the way of discipline, and therefore they perished. And because they did not have the wisdom of God, they perished by their own wisdom. For God, our God, who is the source of life and the true light, the Word and power and wisdom of God, to whom no other can be compared nor is any like found, He discovered every way of discipline, and gave it to Jacob His servant, and to Israel His beloved. After these things, He appeared on earth and lived among men (Baruch 3:36–38). Therefore, all usefulness of discipline and understanding, of wisdom and prudence, must be referred to Him, because every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It is clear that to the eternal power and wisdom of God, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, all things are open, and everything is possible for Him; there is nothing hidden from Him, nor can anything resist His will. But whatever He wishes, He does in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths; He Himself knows the past and judges the future, as He says through the prophet: "Before Me no god was formed, and after Me there will be none" (Isa. 43:10). And in Proverbs: "The Lord," he says, "possessed me at the beginning of His ways, before He made anything from the beginning; I was ordained from eternity, and from ancient times, before He made the earth" (Prov. 8:22-23). And again: "When He prepared the heavens, I was there; when He set a law and circle around the depths, when He established the sky above, and balanced the fountains of waters, when He surrounded the sea with its limit, and set a law for the waters so that they would not pass their boundaries, when He hung the foundations of the earth, I was with Him arranging all things, and I delighted every day, playing before Him" (Prov. 8:27-30). He Himself knows the subtleties of words and the endings of arguments, who in the Gospel said to His disciples: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict" (Luke 21:15). He Himself knows signs and wonders before they happen, and the outcomes of times and ages, who, instructing His chosen ones about the future, foretold to them the signs and wonders which will come before the day of judgment and His coming at the end, therefore saying: "There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, men fainting with fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty," and the rest (Luke 21:25-27).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The wise man, recounting many things about the virtues of wisdom, finally added that he desires to be joined to its company, from which he would have comfort and relief from his weariness; so also the people of the Church, who can truly be said to be king and genuinely wise, because they are members of the heavenly King and Lord, as the apostle Peter says: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Peter 2:9), rejoice in having the communication of divine wisdom, namely of the Lord Jesus Christ, and delight in remaining continually in his embrace and spiritual banquet, whom they know to be most merciful and kind, and the most generous dispenser of heavenly gifts. Therefore, the same speaks in the Apocalypse of Saint John, saying: Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me. To the one who conquers, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne (Rev. 3:20-21). This passage can also be referred to the Virgin Mother of God, who, having the purpose of most chaste virginity within herself, deserved to be made fruitful by the divine word of power, and by giving birth to the Son of God for the salvation of the human race, is to be venerated by all with the proclamation of most celebrated praise. Therefore, she herself says in the song of the Gospel: Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid, for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed (Luke 1:48). To which voice also agree those things which are added in this place.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the birth from the Virgin has been a wonder for all ages, who came, according to the word of blessed Simeon, for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign which would be contradicted. Of whom it is also said through Isaiah: The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, before whom kings will shut their mouths, him the nations will seek, and his tomb shall be glorious (Isa. 11:10). Otherwise, the assembly of holy teachers, filled with the doctrine of the Savior and illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, has brightness before the crowds, when by preaching the Gospel and by recommending the word of God through miracles, it calls together a multitude of the elect from all nations to the faith of God. It has honor among the elders when it subjects the principalities and powers of this world to the Christian religion; or even, according to the mystical sense, it has honor among the elders when it is joined with the patriarchs and prophets in the heavenly kingdom. It is found young and sharp in judgment, when it discerns and judges all things according to the law of God. And it is admirable in the sight of the mighty, when the kings of the earth and princes are amazed at the preaching of the Gospel, and, marveling, revere it, and look upon the speaker, and are unable to resist his argument, as has happened very often, as the book of Acts of the Apostles and the passions of the holy martyrs under the New Testament testify. Therefore, it is read in the aforementioned book that, when Peter was preaching, fear came upon every soul. Many wonders and signs were also done by the apostles in Jerusalem, and great fear was upon all (Acts 1). Similarly, in the same book it is narrated that those who disputed with Stephen could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke (Acts 6). Likewise, Saul, after he received the faith of God and was baptized in Damascus through the preaching of Ananias, grew stronger and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus, affirming that this is the Christ, acting confidently in the name of God (Acts 9). The same apostle, when he was preaching the word of God on the island of Cyprus, and there found a false prophet of the Jews named Bar-Jesus, who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a wise man, when he found that this man was resisting him, he rebuked him and struck him with blindness; immediately the proconsul, when he saw what had happened, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord (Acts 13).
Exposition of the Christian Faith 3.3.18-9

Who would dare deny the immortality of the Son, simply because he has given immortality also to others? Indeed, it is written of the wisdom of God, "Through her I will obtain immortality." But the immortality of his nature is one thing and the immortality of ours another. Perishable things must not be compared with divine things: the being of the divinity is one alone and cannot die. Thus the apostle, though knowing that the soul and the angels are immortal, preached that God alone is immortal. In fact, even the soul dies: "The soul that sins will die." And neither is an angel immortal by nature, because his immortality is dependent on the will of the Creator.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The saints possess immortality, because, instructed by the truth of faith and rooted and grounded in divine love, they are already partakers of the hope of future immortality, and by the teachings of sound doctrine, as well as by the examples of good works with the fruits of virtues, they will leave a blessed memory to the generations that come after them, and deservedly so, because they will have a great multitude of faithful disciples from all nations as preservers of their discipline.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Holy teachers arrange the peoples and the nations subject to them to live with discipline, when they open up and explain to them the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, and make them obey the sacred words of the Gospel. They no longer allow them to wander, wavering through various sects, but compel them to preserve the truth of faith and the purity of doctrine in all things. Even the most savage persecutors and dreadful kings are forced to yield to their patience, because they are in no way able to resist the power of Christ, who works wonders in them. He said to his disciples in the Gospel: "In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, for I have overcome the world" (Jn. 16:33). And again: "He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world." (1 Jn. 4:4) Therefore, among the multitude of the faithful, they appear sincere and kind, but in battle against their adversaries, they are loyal and most courageous. But while these things are done outwardly, let us hear what wisdom grants them inwardly.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

After the preaching of the divine word, after the labors of good works by which holy men outwardly offer comfort to their listeners, returning to the homes of their hearts, they devote themselves in meditation to the contemplation of divine wisdom, and therefore, from the troublesome annoyances of secular affairs, they inwardly attain the peace of heavenly sweetness. For, as it is said, "her company has no bitterness, nor does her companionship bring weariness," because bodily pleasures, when taken greedily, burden the body; but spiritual delights, the more they are received, the more they uplift the mind. For this is the usual difference between the delights of the heart and those of the body: bodily pleasures, when not possessed, kindle a grievous desire; but when greedily consumed, they immediately turn the eater to disgust through filling. On the other hand, spiritual delights, when not possessed, are a source of weariness; but when possessed, they are desired; and the more they are consumed by the one who hungers, the more they are hungered for by the one who consumes. In the former, desire pleases, experience displeases; in the latter, desire is of little value, experience pleases more; in the former, desire produces filling, filling produces disgust; but in the latter, desire produces filling, filling produces desire. For spiritual delights increase their own desire in the mind as they satisfy it, because the more their flavor is perceived, the more it is understood that they are to be loved more eagerly, and therefore, when not possessed, they cannot be loved, because their flavor is unknown.
Against Marivadus the Arian, PL 62

That the Son according to divinity has always been immortal, or is, the divine writings testify everywhere. Solomon affirming the same more clearly: Immortality is in thought wisdom, and the delight of its friendship is good (Wis. 8:17). Likewise there: In the works of the hands of wisdom is honor without failing, and in the contest of his words immortality, and eternal life, in the communication of his words perpetual brightness (Ibid., 18).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Immortality is in the kinship of wisdom, because whatever is truly known about its nature is found to be wholly immortal and always living. In whose friendship, there is good delight; and the more one advances in love for it, the more sweetly one burns with affection for it. In the works of its hands is honor without failure, because it is the origin of all things, and through it all things were created which are in heaven and which are on earth, and which are under the earth. Of which it is written: You have made all things in wisdom (Ps. 104:24). And in the Gospel it says: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it (Jn. 1:3-5). In the contest of its speech, wisdom and brilliance are in the communication of its words, because wisdom itself opens the mouth of the mute, and makes the tongues of infants eloquent. Indeed, I do not want you to seek all these things outside of Christ, for all things that are of God, Christ is: he himself is his wisdom, he himself is strength, he himself is justice, he himself is holiness, and redemption, he himself, to come to the present, is also forethought. But since it is in the underlying, according to the variety of senses, it is called by different names, wisdom signifies one thing, justice another. For when wisdom is spoken of, it institutes the disciplines of divine and human things. When justice, it signifies the distributor and judge of merits. When holiness, that virtue is described which makes believers in God holy. I was going around seeking to take her for myself. This going around signifies the diligence of seeking and the effort of meditating, through which the hearts of the elect strive to attain the knowledge of wisdom. Therefore, also the bride in the Song of Songs says: I will rise and go around the city, through the streets and squares, seeking whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him; the watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves? Scarcely had I passed them, when I found him whom my soul loves (Songs 3:2-4).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

From the Scriptural account of the Kings, we have learned that Solomon, in his youth, asked the Lord for wisdom and a teachable heart so that he might rightly judge the people of the Lord and discern between good and evil, which he obtained, to such an extent that no king before him was like him, nor would any arise after him. Therefore, in a certain way, this statement can be applied to him, because he was granted a good soul, in that he possessed a wise and understanding heart. But it must be considered whether what is added afterwards can pertain to him. Since Scripture itself in many places reproves him, because he loved foreign women, who turned his heart away, and he offended the Lord by building idols for the sake of foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods, therefore it seems to me more fitting, according to the allegory, to refer this to the people of the saints, who, regenerated by the washing of holy baptism and filled with faith in the Savior, received the childhood of good character and similar innocence, and, intent on sacred studies, strive to make progress and to reach the summit of virtues.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

Or do you not know that, when a male child has been made forty days old, he is offered at the altar, that he may there be purified, as one who was polluted in the very conception, whether of the paternal seed or of the maternal womb? Every man, therefore, "is polluted in father and in mother", but Jesus my Lord alone entered clean into this generation, "he was not polluted in his mother". For he entered "an undefiled body". For it was he who had also long ago said through Solomon: "but rather, since I was good, I came to an undefiled body". "He was not" therefore "defiled in his mother", nor even "in his father". For Joseph furnished nothing in his generation except ministry and affection; whence Scripture granted him the appellation of father for his faithful ministry. For thus Mary herself says in the gospel: "behold, I and your father have been seeking you sorrowing". So then this alone is the "great priest" who "was defiled neither in father nor in mother".
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

And when I became better, I came to the defiled body. For the Wisdom of God, which is the unchangeable good, came to the holy and incorrupt virgin, taking from there the defiled body, from which all generations call her blessed. The lover of Wisdom asks God to grant him wisdom, so that he may know what is beneficial before him at all times. And when I became better, I came to a defiled body. For it is written above that the keeping of God's laws is the completion of incorruption, and incorruption makes one to be near to God. But no one can attain to such perfection unless divine grace exalts him. From which, also, the gift of knowledge and the bestowal of virtues are to be sought and hoped for, because, according to the statement of James: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).
SERMON 20:2

"I said, 'Have mercy on me, O Lord. Heal me, for I have sinned against you.' " So—"I said." I do not, to excuse my sin, look for who sinned through me or who forced me to sin. I do not say that it was by chance or that Fate wanted it. And finally, I do not say that it was the devil. Certainly the devil has power to suggest, even to cause fear and even, if he is allowed, to seriously harass. But we must ask the Lord for strength, so that the seductions do not captivate us and the difficulties do not break us. Against the seductions and threats of the enemy he gives us two virtues: continence and patience. To curb pleasures, so that prosperity does not seduce us, and to endure fears, so that difficulties do not break us. "But knowing," it is written, "that no one can be continent unless it is granted him by God," we see that he asked him, "Create a pure heart in me, O God." And also, "Woe to those who have lost the strength to endure."
SERMON 283:2-3

"And this also was wisdom: to know whose gift it was." Therefore, if you have something from God and do not know from whom you have it, you will not receive a reward, since you will be ungrateful for it. If you do not know who gave it to you, you will not give thanks. And if you do not give thanks, you will also lose what you have. Indeed, "to him who has, more will be given." What is it to possess fully? To know from whom it comes. "But the one who does not have," that is, who does not know from whom it comes, "will lose even what he has." Finally, as it also says, "And precisely this was wisdom: to know from whom the gift came." The apostle Paul says this also when he exhorts us to give thanks to God in the Holy Spirit. And almost as if to respond to the question, How will we know the difference? he adds, "that we may know all that has been given to us by God."
SERMONS 30:14

Continence is commanded of us. Where is this command? The apostle writes to Timothy, "Be continent!" It is a command, a precept—we must listen to it and put it into practice. But if God does not help us, we are unable to. We try to do something about it with our will, and the will engages in the attempt. Do not presume to do it without someone to help you in your weakness! You have certainly been commanded to be continent, but listen now to another passage of Scripture: "Knowing that no one can be continent unless God grants it to him, and that it was a gift of wisdom itself to know who was the giver of this gift." So what did he do? He says, "I turned to the Lord and implored him." What need is there, my brothers and sisters, to cite many passages? Whatever command is given us, we must pray so as to be able to carry it out. Clearly not in the sense that we must go off and, as lazy people do, lay on the ground on our backs, saying, "God will rain food in our faces, so we'll have to do absolutely nothing." And then, when food falls in our mouths, we add, "God, stick it in our throats, as well!" We also must do something. We must apply ourselves, we must make an effort, and we must give thanks for what we have been able to do and pray for what we have been unable to do. By thanksgiving, you will avoid being condemned for ingratitude, by asking for what you do not yet have you will avoid being left empty-handed against the obstacles that hinder you.

n: God. This prayer, which continues to the end of the book, is a paraphrase of 3 Kings iii. 6., &c., with several additional instructions, to remind people in authority of the love of justice. (Calmet)

King. Hence it appears, that the sentiments of Solomon are expressed. (Worthington) --- Judge. This is the first duty of a king. --- Thy sons. He ought to govern his people, remembering that they are God's creatures and children.

Beginning. In thy eternal decrees, or when thou madest choice of Israel. (Haydock) --- The temple was greater, but very like the tabernacle: only the court of the priests was divided from that of the people. In the desert, the whole camp was considered a the court of the latter. (Calmet)

With thee. The uncreated wisdom is God himself: that which is communicated to man is his gift, ver. 10. (Worthington) --- World. Proverbs viii. 22. This request shews what idea Solomon had of God's majesty, for which he was preparing a temple.
Thought. How shall we govern as we ought, and act as thy vicegerents, without thy Spirit? (Proverbs xvi. 10., and 2 Kings xiv. 17.)

Whosoever, &c., is not in the Septuagint. But men includes as much. (Haydock) --- The saints have been preserved from the contagion and punishments of the world only by means of the divine benefit. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

In the Gospel, after presenting the example of the one who persistently asked his friend, who was in a room, for three loaves of bread, the Lord immediately turned his speech to the disciples, saying: Ask, and it will be given to you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened (Matt. 7:7-8). Similarly, the apostle James admonishes his hearers to implore wisdom from God, saying: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach, and it will be given to him (James 1:5). From this it is clear that whoever asks rightly, and for those things which are according to God's will, will not be frustrated in the effect of his petition. Therefore, this wise petitioner begs God the Father to give him wisdom, the assistant at his throne, namely that wisdom which always remains with him, and reigns, and can never be separated from him, which is also his Word, through whom all things were made, and man himself, rational, was created in the image of God, so that he might surpass all earthly creatures, and, subject to God, might rule the world placed under him. However, in a higher sense, this can be referred to our Redeemer himself, who, sent by the Father into the world, consented to be born as a man through the Virgin, and who rules and governs the world of the Church by his own will. His judgment never fails, because, as the Prophet testifies: Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faithfulness the belt of his waist (Isa. 11:5). He will judge the world in equity, and the peoples in his truth (Ps. 96:13), who was not rejected but rather chosen by God, of whom it is said through Isaiah: Behold my servant, I will uphold him, my chosen one, my soul delights in him (Isa. 42:1). He also agreed to be called by the name of servant, therefore the divine voice said to him through the aforementioned prophet: It is too small a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to restore the preserved of Israel; I will make you a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isa. 49:6). His mother also did not refuse to profess herself the handmaid of God, who, when the angel announced to her the divine birth in the Gospel, replied: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38). Therefore, the saints are his members, who, reborn by water and the word through the mother Church, and cleansed from the stain of sins by the grace of the Holy Spirit, humbly submit themselves to his service. Therefore, the Son prays to the Father, the head interceding for the body, that it may be enlightened by his grace and led in the way of righteousness; for he knows that whatever good he has in speech, will, and deed is his gift.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 69

For it is to be understood by us not concerning wisdom alone, but concerning every virtue, what Solomon says: "and even if anyone be perfect among the sons of men, if your wisdom be absent from him, he shall be reckoned as nothing". So too whoever has been perfect in chastity or in righteousness or in virtue or in piety, but there has not been in him either the chastity or the righteousness or the virtue or the piety which comes from the grace of God, such a man is reckoned "as nothing". Therefore, if we wish that a more perfect virtue be given to us and abound in us, let us by all means acquire through diligence that which is perfect among men; and after we have acquired it, understanding as it were that these things are reckoned as nothing without the grace of God, let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, and let us pray lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute, so that the perfection of all the good things that are in us may be given from God, and that he may make us perfect and acceptable to God as sons of God.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This is also read in the book of Job: Is not wisdom found among the aged, and does not understanding come with long life? With Him are wisdom and strength; He has counsel and understanding. If He tears down, none can rebuild; if He shuts a man in, none can open (Job 12:12-14). It is clearly evident that human weakness, unless it is sustained by divine help, will fail in countless ways and be reduced to nothing. For by the grace of God we are saved, and every perfect gift comes from above. Aware of this, Paul says of himself: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:24). And again he says: By the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me (1 Cor. 15:10).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The history of the kings narrates that King David, wishing to build a temple, was forbidden by the Lord through the prophet, because his son, who would succeed him in the kingdom, would be the one to build a temple for the Lord; and so it happened that Solomon, who is considered the author of this book, built a wondrous temple for the Lord in Jerusalem. Therefore, now the same king, recalling the benefits of God, asks that His wisdom, through which He made the world, remain with him, and that his actions and heart be directed according to His will. But because the temple itself prefigured the Church of Christ, which the true peacemaker and our King, the Lord Jesus, builds daily through His workers, that is, the holy preachers, for the praise, glory, and honor of His name, we cannot inappropriately transfer these prayers which Solomon offered for himself to the person of the teachers of the holy Church, who know that all things pertaining to the governance of the people of God are not of their own power but of divine gift. Therefore, they also daily ask that He who is the author of every good work may Himself be the giver of supreme perfection. For whatever is written in the divine Scriptures about the wisdom of God, we ought to refer to none other than the mediator between God and men; for He is our peace, who made both one, who is called by the Apostle the power and wisdom of God: the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, because in Him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through Him and in Him, and He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together, and He is the head of the body, the Church; He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that He might have preeminence in all things: because it pleased the Father that in Him all fullness should dwell, and through Him to reconcile all things to Himself, making peace through the blood of His cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven (Col. 1:15-20).
ON THE TRINITY 4:20.28

The Son, therefore, is not properly said to have been sent in that He is begotten of the Father; but either in that the Word made flesh appeared to the world, whence He says, "I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world;" or in that from time to time, He is perceived by the mind of each, according to the saying, "Send her, that, being present with me, she may labor with me." What then is born from eternity is eternal, "for it is the brightness of the everlasting light;" but what is sent from time to time, is that which is apprehended by each. But when the Son of God was made manifest in the flesh, He was sent into this world in the fullness of time, made of a woman. "For after that, in the wisdom of God, the world by wisdom knew not God" (since "the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not"), it "pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe," and that the Word should be made flesh, and dwell among us. But when from time to time He comes forth and is perceived by the mind of each, He is said indeed to be sent, but not into this world; for He does not appear sensibly, that is, He does not present Himself to the corporeal senses. For we ourselves, too, are not in this world, in respect to our grasping with the mind as far as we can that which is eternal.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For all things are naked and open before the eyes of the wisdom of God, nor does any thought escape it; therefore, the one whom it governs, it leads soberly along the path of virtues, and truly protects from the injuries of adversaries, and by making his works acceptable, will render him worthy of the reward of the saints in the heavenly kingdom. But because it belongs to God alone to know what He Himself wills, and He acts in all things by His own command, therefore this praiser of the works of God, suddenly struck with awe, marvels at His greatness.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Whose excellence Paul, amazed, says: O the depth of the riches of wisdom and knowledge, how incomprehensible are His judgments, and unsearchable His ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor? Or who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things; to Him be honor and glory forever and ever (Rom. 11:33-36).
City of God 22.29.4

"And in my flesh I will see God" unquestionably foretells the resurrection of the flesh. It did not say, however, "through my flesh." If it had said this, it would still be possible that Christ was meant by "God," for Christ will be seen by our flesh in the flesh. But, even understanding it of God, it is only equivalent to saying, "I will be in my flesh when I see God." And the apostle's phrase, "face to face" does not lead us to believe that we will see God with the face of this body, in which we have our bodily eyes. Rather, we will see him continuously with the mind. If the face were not also that of the interior person, the apostle would not say, "And we, with unveiled faces, seeing as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, will be transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the action of the Spirit of the Lord." Nor do we interpret differently what is proclaimed in a psalm, "Draw near to him, and you will be enlightened, and your faces will not blush with shame." One draws near to God by faith, which is certainly of the heart, not the body. But we are not unaware of the valid reasons that the spiritual body has for drawing near to the Lord, since we speak of a reality outside our experience, and because in this matter an authoritative passage of sacred Scripture that can be interpreted unequivocally does not come to mind or help us. Thus, necessarily, what we read in the book of Wisdom is also true of us: "The reasonings of mortals are timid and our reflections uncertain."
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore the thoughts of mortals are timid, because they are fragile, and therefore the foresight of man is uncertain, because his soul is changeable, and his flesh is corruptible, as the following sentence shows.
SERMONS 95:5

Next the Lord says: "blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth by inheritance." To the meek and gentle, to the humble and modest, and to those who are prepared to endure all injuries, the earth is promised for their possession. And this is not to be reckoned a small or cheap inheritance, as if it were distinct from our heavenly dwelling, since it is no other than these who are understood to enter the kingdom of heaven. The earth, then, which is promised to the meek, and is to be given to the gentle in possession, is the flesh of the saints, which in reward for their humility will be changed in a happy resurrection, and clothed with the glory of immortality, in nothing now to act contrary to the spirit, and to be in complete unity and agreement with the will of the soul. For then the outer man will be the peaceful and unblemished possession of the inner man: then the mind, engrossed in beholding God, will be hampered by no obstacles of human weakness nor will it any more have to be said "The body which is corrupted, weigheth upon the soul, and its earthly house presseth down the sense which thinketh many things:" for the earth will not struggle against its tenant, and will not venture on any insubordination against the rule of its governor. For the meek shall possess it in perpetual peace, and nothing shall be taken from their rights, "when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality:" that their danger may turn into reward, and what was a burden become an honour.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Blessed is the man who is always fearful (Prov. 28:14), and does not presume to think, speak, or act at any time. On the contrary, the foolish people of heretics are confident and ensnared, caught by their own words; therefore Scripture says: But he who is stubborn of mind will fall into evil (Ibid.). For it is fitting for the servant of God to deal soberly with earthly things and cautiously with heavenly things, and let him remember what is written: Do not seek things that are too high for you; God made all good things in their own time, and handed over the world to their conflict, so that man may not find the work which God has done from the beginning to the end (Eccles. 3:11). And elsewhere: I applied, he says, my heart to know wisdom, and to understand the dispensation that is at work on earth; and I understood that of all the works of God, no man can find the reason for those things which are done under the sun: and the more he labored to seek, the less he would find. Even if the wise man says he knows, he will not be able to find it (Eccles. 8:16–17). Therefore it is rightly said here: What is in view we find with labor, but what is in the heavens, who has investigated? But lest he should cause us to despair of inquiring into divine things, he brings us consolation by adding the grace of the Holy Spirit.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

But who has known your mind, unless you have given him wisdom, and sent your Holy Spirit from on high? For it is clear that we can only perceive knowledge of divine things through the grace of the Holy Spirit, because no one knows what is in a man except the spirit of the man which is in him. So also, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God; he himself enlightens the hearts of the saints, and instructs them about invisible and heavenly things, so that they may perceive the understanding of the divine majesty according to their capacity, and are always compelled to love his goodness. For by wisdom all those who pleased you, Lord, from the beginning have been healed. Now he begins to explain that through the wisdom of God, that is, Christ, all who pleased God have been healed.

n: Sin. Hence it is clear, that our first parent repented, (Worthington) and was saved, Genesis v. 5. (St. Irenæus iii. 34.; St. Augustine, ep. xcix. ad Evod.; Cornelius a Lapide) (Calmet) --- Things. Before sin, he submitted willingly; but afterwards, he was forced to use all his ingenuity to preserve this dominion.
The unjust. Cain. We have no proof of his repentance.

Cause. The wickedness of the race of Cain. (Calmet) --- Just. Noe[Noah]. --- Wood. Who would have thought that such a vessel would save mankind, &c., amid the raging storms? Noe must have been an able mechanic: (Calmet) but God both directed him, and closed up the door, Genesis vii. 16. (Haydock)

She knew the just. She found out and approved Abraham, (Calmet) Sem, or Heber, who took no part in building the tower. (St. Augustine, City of God) (Chap. xvi. 4.) --- To God. Many say that Abraham was at first addicted to idolatry. (Philo.) (St. Augustine, &c.) --- But not after he was directed by the light of heaven. (Calmet) --- Strong. Gave him strength to stand firm against the efforts of his natural tenderness, when he was ordered to sacrifice his son. (Challoner) --- Against. Literally, "in." To obey God was true compassion to his son, though it might have deprived him of this life. (Haydock) --- How many virtues did not Abraham manifest on this occasion! (St. Ambrose, Off. ii. 5.)
The just man. Lot. --- Pentapolis. The land of the five cities, Sodom, Gomorrah, &c. (Challoner)
The just. Jacob. --- Of God. Or heaven open, and angels ascending and descending, Genesis xxxviii. 12.
Deceit. Laban's craft did not prevent Jacob from growing rich. (Haydock)
Enemies. Laban and Esau. (Calmet) --- Conflict with the angel. (Challoner)

Just. Joseph. (Challoner) --- Sinners. His brethren, &c. Septuagint, "from sin" of adultery. (Menochius) --- Pit. Or prison, to which he was confined at the instigation of Potiphar's wife, always preserving his virtue. (Calmet) --- He had also been let down into an old pit by his brethren. (Haydock)
Kingdom. Which he ruled under Pharao, Genesis xli. 40. (Calmet) --- The Hebrews styled all in high authority kings. (Grotius)
God. Moses. (Challoner) --- Numbers xii. 7., and Psalm civ. 26., &c.

Eloquent. They would, if possible, have sounded forth thy praise. (Dionysius) --- The Hebrews had been kept in ignorance, and afraid to speak. (Calmet) --- Infants, and dumb people, might also, by miracle, join in the song. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

By the goodness of the Creator, the first man was created and placed in paradise, and by the order of his Maker, he was set above all living creatures, so that Scripture relates that after all the creatures of the earth and all the birds of the sky were formed, God brought them to Adam to see what he would call them, and Adam named all the animals, all the birds of the sky, and all the beasts of the earth (Gen. 11). But when, because of the transgression of the command, he was cast out of paradise and plunged into the misery of this world, he was again restored through divine wisdom, through which he was first created, that is, Christ; and this is the sign of the great mercy of almighty God, that He decided to restore the man who, having been deceived by another's persuasion, fell into sin, so that His work would not perish, which from the beginning He had made in His own image and likeness. For He made the nations of the world able to be healed (Wis. 1), and He who did not do evil, lest His work should become worthless, that is, lest His work in man should utterly perish.
Sermon 159B

Man was indeed made in the image of God, and as it is written elsewhere, He gave him the power of containing all things: everything was under him, but above him was the One who made all things. Thus, man ought to have regarded those things that were under him, so that he might more regard the One who was above him; for clinging to the superior, he would more securely possess the inferior; but departing from the superior, he would be subjected to the inferior. Just as if we suppose three men: one man having a servant and a master, as often happens that peculiar servants have servants. Consider this: he has a servant, he has a master; subject to one, superior to another; he is superior to the servant, inferior to his master. We have placed a third as the servant of a servant, but the first as the master of a master, and the middle one both servant and master: master of his servant and servant of his master. That third is only a servant, the first is only a master, the middle one is both a servant and a master. And he securely possesses his servant if he does not offend his master. And, indeed, we have mentioned three men: all are of the same kind, all subsist from the same substance and nature. Not so are those three: God, man, and the creature inferior to man. For the Creator and the created, the maker and the made, the craftsman and the work, the creator and the creature are of a different kind and not of the same substance. However, those things which were created are generally called created things, but they differ by natures, orders, merits, and places.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He denotes the first offspring of Adam, that is, Cain, who through the wickedness of envy departed from God and unjustly killed his brother Abel, bringing about his own destruction. When the punishment for this crime was exacted in the flood and the generation of Cain was destroyed, divine wisdom again, through the construction of the ark, preserved Noah, descending from the line of Seth, together with his sons, for the restoration of the world, as the following statement demonstrates:
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

But in a higher sense, wisdom, governing the righteous through a humble piece of wood, restored the human race, when through the passion of Christ's cross it erased the sin of the whole world and led the chosen to the entrance of the heavenly kingdom. But again, after the cleansing of the flood, it then adds what wisdom accomplished as a wondrous work:
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

After the Devil, through pride, deceived the human race in the building of the tower, so that by this transgression the unity of the common language was lost, again the wisdom of God united the offspring of Abraham in the truth of his faith, giving him a law and worship in which they might prove themselves to be true worshipers of the one God. From his seed also, producing the redemption of the human race, He blessed in him all the nations of the earth, and therefore what the pride of the Devil had confounded, the humility of Christ, through His grace, reunited in the knowledge and speech of all languages.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This opinion was in a certain way explained by the blessed Peter in his Epistle concerning the justice of God, writing thus: "He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction by reducing them to ashes, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly; and he rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the evil conduct of the lawless. For that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment," etc. (2 Peter 2:6-9) The story is well known, how God sent fire upon Pentapolis and justly condemned the sinful cities, turning the most fertile land into a wilderness, so that it no longer yields any fruit, showing that the souls damned in hell will burn forever without the fruit of repentance. For when Lot fled from there and headed for the mountains, his wife, because she looked back and did not persevere in her begun journey, is said to have been turned into a pillar of salt. This mystically warns us that those who have been regenerated by the grace of God and called to eternal life should not look back to the old way of life, nor remain foolishly midway. The fact that Lot's wife looked back and remained, and was turned into salt, serves as an example for the seasoning of the faithful, by which others may be salted; for Christ did not keep this silent, saying, "Remember Lot's wife," (Luke 17:32) namely, that he might season us as with salt, so that we might not neglect as fools, but be wise and beware. This, too, she admonished when she was turned into a pillar of salt. But the wisdom of God frees those who observe Him from all sorrows and preserves them perpetually in the peace of eternal rest.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This passage, although it may seem to pertain specifically to the patriarch Jacob according to the historical account, who, fleeing his brother Esau, went to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia, where on the journey he saw in a dream a ladder set up, and the angels of God descending and ascending on it, and the Lord leaning on the ladder, saying to him: I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac; the land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your descendants (Gen. 28:13), and upon arriving in Mesopotamia, he took Leah and Rachel, the daughters of his uncle, as wives, for whom he also tended his sheep for a very long time. But although that man tried to deprive him of his wages through deceit, he was kept unharmed by the wisdom of God, and returned to his homeland enriched with great wealth.
