More generally, however, according to the allegorical interpretation, it pertains to the holy martyrs, whom the divine wisdom, namely Christ our Lord, by His mercy delivered from all persecutions of their enemies, and protected them unblemished from their snares, strengthening them by the grace of the Holy Spirit and the hope of future reward, and finally, with all their enemies defeated, led them as most blessed victors to the eternal kingdom, so that there they might forever sing praises to Him, by whose help they knew themselves to have been preserved and saved.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The story of the patriarch Joseph seems to recount both his slanders and later happiness, who, having been sold by his brothers, was brought to Egypt, and there, because of the accusation of his master's wife, was sent to prison, therefore, due to his interpretation of dreams, he was brought out by order of Pharaoh and made ruler of Egypt. But just as the wisdom of God delivered him from the hands of his enemies and made him lord of the land, so also, in a special way, He rescued the holy martyrs from the punishments of their persecutors and exalted them in the heavenly kingdom, where, enjoying eternal glory, they will come as judges with Christ over their enemies, so that they may assign to them eternal punishments for their crimes and lies.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He calls a just people and a seed without complaint the people of Israel, who, descending from the seed of the patriarchs, became worshippers of the one God, but were oppressed by the Egyptians and other nations. Through the leadership of Moses and Aaron, they were delivered from there and exalted by the wonders of God, that is, by the crossing of the Red Sea, by the protection of the cloud by day, the brilliance of fire by night, and by the other miracles that were abundantly performed among them in the desert. Mystically, however, the Lord delivers his chosen ones from the hands of their persecutors, and through the flashing of miracles terrifies their adversaries, and gives his servants wisdom which none of their adversaries will be able to resist or contradict. Therefore, even before kings and powers of this world, they stand unafraid, confidently speaking the word of God, and through the suffering of the martyrs, they attain the rewards of the heavenly kingdom, where perpetually and without end they sing worthy praises to their King and Deliverer.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It is clear that without the wisdom of God, the human mind can neither conceive anything worthy nor utter anything fitting; therefore, sober understanding and the ability of sound speech must be sought from Him alone, since all things are from Him, through Him, and in Him.

n: Prophet. Moses, (Challoner) by whose ministry the Hebrews were delivered, (Haydock) and governed with the utmost prudence, Numbers xii. 26. (Calmet)
Their enemies. The Amalecites, (Challoner) and all others, who durst attack Moses, Deuteronomy iii. 1.

By what things, &c. The meaning is, that God, who wrought a miracle to punish the Egyptians by thirst, when he turned all their waters into blood, (at which time the Israelites, who were exempt from those plagues, had plenty of water) wrought another miracle in favour of his own people in their thirst, by giving them water out of the rock. (Challoner) --- The Egyptians were thus tormented with thirst, though so near the Nile; and the Hebrews were refreshed in a barren desert, Exodus vii. 20.
River. The Nile, to which the Egyptians gave divine honours. (Calmet) --- Thou. Septuagint, "disturbed with corrupted blood, in punishment of the infanticide decree, thou gavest," &c.

By their punishments, &c. That is, that the Israelites had been benefited and miraculously favoured in the same kind, in which they had been punished. (Challoner) --- Benefited. After war, peace is more agreeable. (Worthington)
Serpents. The Egyptians adored asps, and fed them at their tables, without receiving any harm. (Ælian. Hist. xvii. 5.) --- Dumb beasts. Viz., frogs, sciniphs, flies, and locusts. (Challoner)
Repentance. If people neglect to reform their conduct in this world, they must expect to be treated with all severity in the other.
It. Sin and disorder is the work of man, deserving hatred. (Calmet) --- God created nothing evil, nor is there any but one God, as the Manichees pretended. (Worthington)
Called. Into existence, or into its proper place, Romans iv. 17.
All. Awaiting their amendment, and unwilling to destroy thy creatures, chap. xii. 10. Hence thou didst not exterminate the Egyptians at once. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The former people, departing from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, journeyed through the deserts and pitched their tents in uninhabitable places, as the history of the Pentateuch recounts. In the same way, the people who follow now, that is, the Christians, journey through the desert of this world under the guidance of prophecy, so that, with Christ reigning, they may reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom. This is also clearly stated by the Apostle Peter, who says: We have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts (2 Peter 1:19).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

But what that rock signified, from which the Israelites drank, Paul testifies, saying: "They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:4). This rock, struck by the rod of the cross, which was foretold in the hands, that is, in the writings of the prophets, poured forth living water which fills all the elect and satisfies them with eternal fulfillment. Therefore, Truth itself says: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn. 7:37-38). And elsewhere: "Whoever drinks the water that I will give him, it will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (Jn. 4:14). Therefore, this rock is called the highest because in it is contained the most abundant grace of the Holy Spirit; it is called a hard stone because it is firm and stable, upon which every wise man builds his house so that it is not moved by any storm. Concerning this, Moses also says in the song of Deuteronomy: "They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hard stone" (Deut. 32:13). Nowhere is such a thing read in the history; if the whole sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed, nowhere did the people suck honey from the rock, nowhere did they suck oil. But because, according to Paul's word, the rock was Christ, they sucked honey from the rock who saw the deeds and miracles of our Redeemer. But they sucked oil from the hard stone who, after his resurrection, deserved to be anointed by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; as if, therefore, the hard stone gave honey when the Lord, still mortal, showed the sweetness of his miracles to the disciples. But the hard stone poured out oil because, after his resurrection, now made obstructed, he poured forth the gift of holy anointing through the breathing of the Spirit. Of this oil it is said through the prophet: "The yoke will rot because of the oil" (Isa. 10:27). Indeed, we were held under the yoke of demonic domination, but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit, and because the grace of liberty has anointed us, the yoke of demonic domination has rotted.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He commemorates the blessings of God, which were bestowed upon the former people through divine mercy, when, as they thirsted, He brought forth water from the rock and refreshed them with abundant drink. Likewise, on the contrary, he recounts the punishments which their enemies suffered in the slaughter of their firstborn and the various calamities that, by the just judgment of God, came upon them. Mystically, however, it signifies that the people of God and the sheep of His pasture, whom the supreme shepherd redeemed at the price of His own blood, quench their thirst at the fountain of living water, and their persecutors, failing in eternal want, will be delivered to perpetual death. Similar to this is that which the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah against His adversaries, saying: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart, and shall wail for breaking of spirit (Isa. 65:13-14). But that drink is to be understood here, which will spring from the fountains of Israel, which whoever drinks will have within himself a fountain of water springing up into eternal life, which also the Savior promises to drink with the apostles in the kingdom of the Father, which gladdens the heart of man, so that those who drink may say: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. 5:6). And the mother of the Lord, full of the Holy Spirit, prophesied: He has filled the hungry with good things, who previously did not have the food of the Lord, and the rich He has sent away empty (Luke 1:53), who were given for His burial, and whom, though they promised a prophet, they rejected. Concerning whom also in another place the Psalmist sings: The rich have lacked and suffered hunger (Ps. 30:10), that is, the people of the Jews. But those who seek the Lord, that is, the multitude of the Gentiles, will not lack any good thing. And when those serving Christ and believing in Him shall have rejoiced and praised the Lord for gladness of heart and joy, then those others will be put to shame, seeing others received into their place, and will cry out for pain of heart, fulfilling that which is written: There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 13:42), when the lambs of the Gentiles and the righteous will stand at the right hand, and the goats of the Jews and the wicked at the left, the former receiving eternal rewards, the latter everlasting punishments. But the regret of spirit, through pain of heart, is to be understood in the conscience of sinners, according to that which is written: Those who err in spirit will come to understanding (Isa. 29:24), and a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps. 51:17). The spirit is crushed when it is lifted up, as is written of the wicked king of Israel: The Lord hardened his spirit. And of the prince of the Babylonians, when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened, so that in pride he said: This is Babylon, and I have made it (Dan. 5:20).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Whoever examines the reading of the Old Testament carefully, easily recognizes how God frequently chastised the Israelites, who sinned often, with deserved punishments, and again, when they repented, comforted them with timely comfort. However, as for foreigners, that is, the Egyptians and the Canaanites, judging them unworthy of His mercy, He exterminated them with harsh vengeance.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

What is said, that both the absent and the present were similarly tormented, either signifies according to history that not only those Egyptians who were present with Pharaoh before Moses and Aaron were struck by the ten plagues, but also all the others who dwelled throughout the land of Egypt were similarly punished; or it refers to the time when not only those whom the Israelites destroyed in each city by recent calamity suffered penalties, but also all the nations of the land of the Canaanites, hearing indeed the victory of the people of God and the power of the signs which were performed at their departure by the will of the Lord, were greatly terrified by them. This is also shown by the words spoken by Rahab the prostitute to the spies of Joshua: "I know," she said, "that the Lord has given you the land; indeed, your terror has fallen upon us, and all the inhabitants of the land have suffered. We have heard how the Lord dried up the waters of the Red Sea at your entrance, when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, Sihon and Og, whom you destroyed. And hearing these things, we feared, and our hearts suffered, nor did any spirit remain in us at your entrance. For the Lord your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath" (Josh. 2:9-11). But although these things were done among the former people in the times of the law, nevertheless, conversely, the Jews who despised the incarnation of the Son of God and refused to accept His preaching, not only within their homeland but also wandering and exiled throughout the whole world, are tormented by various calamities; and the nations who received the faith of God and were converted from their idols to the true worship of the one God, when they sin, accepting paternal correction, are never cast away from the mercy of God. This is the change of the right hand of the Most High, so that those who were once the head now become the tail, and those who were once the tail now become the head. Lebanon has been turned into Carmel, and Carmel has been reckoned as a forest. The Lord is just in all His ways, and holy in all His works (Isa. 29); for therefore the first shall be last, and the last shall be first (Matt. 20:16).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The misery of the wicked is twofold, when the memory of past evils is not diminished, and the storm of present tribulations increases. Therefore, they have no hope of remedy in the future, because although they may fake repentance for their sins, they have no real intention of improving their ways. Therefore, it is written of the Jews in Psalm 79: When He slew them, then they sought Him, and they returned and sought God early; and they remembered that God was their helper, and the Most High God was their redeemer. And they loved Him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to Him, but their heart was not right with Him, nor were they steadfast in His covenant. (Ps. 78:34-37) He does not act in the same way toward the just. Why does He not do the same to them? Because they do not sin in the same way. For the just man falls seven times and rises again; but the wicked shall fall into evil (Prov. 24:16). For when the wicked has come into the depth of evils, he despises.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

But for their senseless thoughts, their iniquities. According to their hardness and impenitent heart, they are storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, for a hard heart will fare badly (Rom. 2:5). In the end, judgments are prepared for mockers and sinners will pursue evil, but good will be repaid to the just (Prov. 19:29). Was not at a loss to send upon them a multitude of bears or bold lions or newly created beasts full of rage, unknown, either breathing a fiery breath or hissing clouds of smoke or flashing terrible sparks from their eyes. It was fitting that those who worshipped the creature instead of the Creator should receive vengeance from the very source from which they sought help. For the world itself fights against the senseless on His behalf. But since in the history of the Old Testament these types of unknown beasts, which are listed, are nowhere else mentioned as being expressed, so that such monsters would punish sinners, it is better to transfer this to a spiritual sense, so that we may understand that all idol worshippers, as well as heretics and schismatics, who follow the sects of their errors as if they were truth, are deservedly punished by spiritual beasts, that is, by unclean spirits, from whom the Prophet prays that faithful souls may be delivered by divine grace: "Do not give the souls who confess to you to the beasts" (Ps. 74:19). Their appearance is terrifying, their cruelty excessive, and their rage immense, because their entire intention is to pursue the human race with hatred and to bring them to be tormented with themselves in the torments of Hades. But since God condemns no one unjustly, and subjects no one to punishment undeservedly. But you have arranged all things in measure, number, and weight. For He does all things according to truth, judgment, and justice, and there is nothing disordered or inappropriate in His works and deeds, but He moderates and arranges all His judgments by the balance of the highest equity. This statement can also be applied to the condition of all creatures; because the almighty Creator made all His works, which He created from the beginning, with a definite number, measure, and weight. Of Him it is written: He counts the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by their names (Ps. 147:4). Therefore also it is read in Job: For He looks to the ends of the earth, and sees all things under the heavens, who made a weight for the winds, and measured the waters, when He gave the rain its law, and a path for the thunderstorm (Job 28:24-26). Therefore also it is said by someone: All things whatsoever have been constructed from the primeval nature of things seem to be formed by the principle of numbers, for this was the chief pattern in the mind of the Creator. Therefore the multitude of the four elements was changed, therefore the succession of times, therefore the motions of the stars and the revolution of the heavens. Since these things are so, and since the state of all things is shaped by the connection of numbers, it is also necessary that number itself always remains in its own substance equally. Who then is sufficient to comprehend this measure, this number, and this weight of God, so as to be able to describe all His arrangements under these three definitions? In measure, I think, consists quality; in number, quantity; in weight, proportion. These are balanced in the judgment and mercy of God, because they are enclosed within these two holy boundaries, by which He established, governs, and will judge the world; in these, God the just Judge cannot be comprehended, cannot be reproved. Therefore, all that we have said above, or will say, now lie hidden from us within the enclosure of these three: which will then be unlocked only by the keys of God's judgment and mercy, so that they may be known, when at the coming of the Lord they will be revealed, so that praise or punishment may be from God to each one.
Questions on the Old and New Testaments, PL 35

In Wisdom, it says, He who created the world from formless matter: and on the other hand, because we were made from nothing (Wis. 11:18, and Gen. 1:2). That God created confused substances at once, the sense of the Scriptures declares, with darkness, indeed, mingled. He called this confusion of things, that is, air, fire, water, earth, darkness, formless matter, as it is read in Genesis: But the earth was, he says, invisible and unformed (Gen. 1:2). From this confusion therefore He created the world by the established firmament, so that within it, with the waters gathered together into one, there might be a dwelling place for the human race. For the substances having been distinguished and separated, He made in the hollow a habitable home.
Confessions 12.8.8

But the "heaven of the heavens" belongs to you, Lord. And the earth that you assigned "to the children of mortals," for them to see and to touch, was not the one that we now see and touch. "It was invisible and confused," an abyss, on which no light shone. In other words, "darkness ruled over the abyss," that is, a darkness greater than that in the abyss. The abyss today, of visible waters, even in their depths have a semblance of light, perceivable in any case by fish and by the animals that crawl on the ocean floor. That other, rather, was altogether virtually nothing, because it was still absolutely without form. It was, however, such as could assume a form. You, Lord, brought forth "the world from unformed matter"—what was almost nothing, drawn by you out of nothing, to bring forth the great things that we human beings admire. This is truly the marvel of these corporeal heavens, that is, of the firmament, which you created between the waters on the second day, after the light was created, saying, "Let it be so. And so it was."
QUESTIONS FROM THE OLD TESTAMENT 2:20

In Wisdom it says, "He who created the world from formless matter," and the opposite, "We were made from nothing." The sense of Scripture affirms that God created the elements all at once, with darkness also mixed in with them. And God called this confusion of elements (that is, air, fire, water, land and darkness) formless matter, as it says in Genesis: "The earth, moreover, was invisible and formless." And from this confusion he then created the world, also establishing the firmament, so that, once the waters were gathered in a single place, it might be the dwelling of the human race. Having distinguished and separated the elements, he made an inhabitable dwelling in the cavity that remained.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 20: HE CREATED THE WORLD FROM UNSEEN MATTER

IN WISDOM IT SAYS, “HE CREATED, IT SAYS, THE WORLD FROM UNSEEN MATTER”; AND ELSEWHERE, THAT WE HAVE BEEN MADE FROM NOTHING (Wis. 11:18 and 2:2). — That God created confused substances at the same time is shown by the meaning of the Scriptures, with darkness of course being mixed in. He called this confusion of things, that is, air, fire, water, earth, darkness, unseen matter, just as it is read in Genesis: “Now the earth, he says, was invisible and without form” (Gen. 1:2). From this confusion, therefore, he created the world by establishing the firmament, so that, with the waters gathered together within it into one place, a dwelling might be made for the human race. For when the substances had been distinguished and separated, he made in the hollow space a habitable home.
The Six Days of Creation, Book 2, PL 14

Therefore, because fire overflows and boils, water also overflowed on the earth, lest the heat of the rising sun and the burning stars should scorch it, and an unusual vapor should harm the tender beginnings of things. How many springs, rivers, and lakes water the lands; is it not because some internal fire sends up vapor within them? For from where would trees sprout, or grain and crops break forth or be ripened, unless an inner fire also gave them life? This fire is often struck out from stones, and frequently leaps out even from wood itself when it is being cut. Therefore, just as the creation of fire is necessary so that things may remain ordered and arranged, and the kindness of heaven may temper the harshness of the waters; so also the abundance of waters is not superfluous, lest one should consume the other, because unless there is a suitable measure of each, just as fire dries up water, so also water extinguishes fire. And so He has weighed and measured all things; for even the drops of rain are numbered for Him, as we read in the book of Job (Job 28:25). Knowing that there would easily be either a lack of things or the dissolution of the universe if one should prevail over the other, He has so balanced the losses of both; that fire should not consume too much, nor water overflow: but there should be a moderate reduction of each, which would remove the excess and preserve what is necessary.
Questions, PL 89

Weight and measure govern and administer all things by the Lord. For when He had set the limit of life to one hundred and twenty years for those who lived in the time of Noah, after He saw sin increase and overflow, He did not wait for the prescribed limit, but cut it short and made it briefer, and in the hundredth year brought the flood upon all. So also to Abraham, He foretold that his offspring would be strangers, and He teaches the reason. For He says, the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to this point. They have not yet, He says, committed those sins which deserve to perish utterly; therefore I will not allow them to be handed over to you to be completely destroyed now, but I await the measure of iniquity. For our sins, which occur in time, fall under a measure, up to a certain quantity; and now our righteous Judge God inflicts punishments, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Nothing is impossible for the Almighty, therefore no one can resist Him; for all things are placed in the will of the Lord, and there is no one who can resist His will. Whatever God willed, He did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the depths. Therefore, the arm of the Lord is none other than the only-begotten Son of God, to whom it is said through Isaiah: Arise, arise, put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the ancient days, in generations of old. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon? etc. (Isa. 51:9). The prophet speaks on behalf of the people to the arm of the Lord, and requests His coming, so that He who for many ages delivered His saints from dangers, now coming in person may defend His chosen ones from their enemies.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Similar to this statement is what is read in Isaiah: Behold, the nations are as a drop from a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance (Isa. 40:15). And a little later: All the nations, he says, are as nothing before him, and are accounted by him as nothing and emptiness. (Isa. 40:17) This is meant to be understood as that the mind and reason and sense of the Lord, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made, is the one of whom it is sung in the psalms: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of his mouth (Ps. 33:6). All the nations who do not know their creator, or the whole of mankind in comparison to God, are as a drop from a bucket and as the small dust of the balance, which with slight weight inclines to the other side; and just as the early morning dew-drop, which is easily dried when the sun rises, or as if a small drop flows from a bucket and is disregarded by the one carrying it, so the entire multitude of the nations, when compared to the heavenly splendor, and the ministries above, and the multitude of angels, is considered as nothing.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, the power of God, always joined with goodness, although it is in need of nothing, nevertheless does not despise His work in men on account of their sins, but by granting forgiveness through repentance, He washes them from sins, and with fatherly compassion, He encourages and nourishes them to be gathered back to Himself.
COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 3

let us take our example from God Himself. For He loves all things that are, equally, so that He hates none of the things He has made; for neither did He make anything that He would hold in hatred: not however for this reason did He love the Egyptians alike as the Hebrews, and Pharaoh as Moses and Aaron. Nor again did He love the rest of the sons of Israel alike as Moses and Aaron and Miriam; nor again did He love Aaron and Miriam alike as Moses, although it be true what is said to Him: "But You spare all, because they are Yours, O Lord, lover of souls; for the spirit of incorruption is in all things"; nevertheless He who disposed all things by measure and number and weight, according to the measure without doubt of each one tempers the balance also of His love. Shall we suppose that Paul was not loved by Him alike when he was persecuting the Church of God, and when he was loved while he himself was bearing persecutions and torments for her, and was saying that there was in him the solicitude of all the Churches?
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The good worker loves, preserves, and governs good work, and therefore, if ever human weakness strays from the way of truth by sinning, he endures with much patience, waiting for them to be converted for the better through repentance. Therefore, he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45). But those who abuse the patience of God and do not turn to repentance are condemned by his just judgment, because the Lord is just and loves justice; his face has seen equity (Ps. 11:7).

Pardon. Or impunity. (Calmet) --- "Thou art angry, and yet are tranquil.["] (St. Augustine, Confessions i. 4.)
Done? Shall the clay say to the potter, why hast thou made me thus? (Isaias xlv. 9., and lxiv. 8.) We know, that under a just God, no one is miserable, unless he deserve it, ver. 15.

Hope. Under a God of such clemency, none should despair.

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the Spirit of God is gentle, for He Himself is the love of God, and the giver of all good; He Himself reproves men, because He causes those whom He fills to reprove sinners, just as Truth itself says to the disciples in the Gospel: I tell you the truth, it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you. And when He comes, He will convict the world concerning sin, and righteousness, and judgment. Concerning sin, because they do not believe in Me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see Me no longer; concerning judgment, because the prince of this world is judged (Jn. 16:7-11). Blessed is the man who hears the voice of this Teacher and obeys His commands, for he will be the possessor of the heavenly kingdom.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It commemorates historically how the seven nations, which had possessed the land of the Canaanites, were driven out of their places by the Lord because of the infidelity and injustices they had committed, and how the children of Israel, namely the worshippers of His name, were brought into their place. Mystically, however, those seven most wicked nations signify the universality of vices which, after the transgression of the first man, began to possess the human race, but through the grace of Christ were expelled from the hearts of the faithful, and the multitude of sacred virtues was introduced there, so that, with the evil possessors expelled from the land of souls by the Gospel of Christ, legitimate inhabitants, that is, the fruits of virtues, might produce vital shoots there by the working of the Holy Spirit. If anyone thinks it necessary to ask how it is said that the Lord sent wasps before His army into the most depraved nations, so that they might gradually exterminate them, when nowhere in the history of the Old Testament is it read that this happened physically, let him know that many things can happen there in the punishment of the wicked, which the writer of history did not care to express throughout, or rather that wasps are placed here in a figurative expression for the terrors which the Israelites, fighting against the surrounding nations, brought upon them. For the fame of those wars, which were accomplished by the power of the Lord, pierced the hearts of the fearful with the sharpest stings of terror, so that it utterly destroyed in them all strength to resist, and this lasted as long as they faithfully rendered worship to God. But after they sinned and neglected to serve God, they were delivered into the hands of their enemies, so that those who had previously been subject to them afterwards became their superiors.
1 CLEMENT 7:5-7

We look over all the generations, and we note that from generation to generation the Master "gave room for repentance" for all those who wanted to turn to him. Noah preached repentance, and all who listened to him were saved. Jonah predicted the destruction of the Ninevites, but, repentant for their sins, God looked favorably on them, and they received salvation, though they were foreigners to God.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He clearly shows by reason that in no way should it be attributed to the Creator that He disposes of His creature according to His own will. For all things are placed in His will, and there is none who can resist His will (Esther 13). Therefore, it is said by Paul: O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: Why did you make me? Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? (Rom. 9:20-21) For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things: but the Lord is just in all His ways, and holy in all His works. (Ps. 145:17)
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

What is it that condemns him who ought not to be punished, since the condemnation itself is certainly punishment; but here he uses “punish” for “correct,” as if he were saying: He who does not accept correction will receive correction, he justly condemns to eternal fire him who is outside the power of God, that is, unworthy of divine mercy. For the power of God is the beginning of justice; because the judgment of God, whether in the correction of the elect or in the condemnation of the reprobate, is the highest perfection of equity, and therefore, through His goodness, He delays judgment for a long time so that He may have more to whom He can render benefit. For when the creature, in its pride, raises itself against its Creator, it does not wish to be subject to His dominion; indeed, just punishment avenges, lest the creation seem to prevail against its Maker. This passage can also be aptly transferred to the passion of our Redeemer, whom the Father delivered up to death for us. But it must be considered how He is just and arranges all things justly, if He condemns him who ought not to be punished. Our Mediator ought not to be punished for Himself, because He committed no contagion of guilt, but if He had not taken upon Himself an undeserved death, He would never have freed us from deserved death. Therefore, since the Father is just, punishing the Just One, He arranges all things justly, because by this He justifies all things, in that He condemns Him who is without sin for sinners, so that all the elect might rise to the summit of justice by Him who, above all, endured the condemnation of our injustice.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For divinity indeed shows its power in the correction of wrongdoers, so that the stubbornness of the proud may not presume upon its own strength; yet it will do so without any passion or disturbance, because God is impassible, and is never changed by any alteration, but always remaining the same, He renews, arranges, and orders all things, as the following statement proves.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the Almighty God judges all things with the peacefulness of His nature, but in the patient vengeance of God He seems to restrain His anger, which in fact does not exist, but human emotions, just as bodily members, are ascribed to God in figurative language, so that the divine words may be adapted to our manner and understanding. Therefore, it is also read in the Scriptures: the eyes of God, and ears, mouth, hands and feet, anger and fury, and other emotions which are diverse in men, whereas the simple nature has no division, nor does true unity admit any division, but the one and the same God always works diverse and varied works, of whom it is said through the Prophet: All things shall grow old like a garment, and as a clothing you will change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail (Ps. 102:25-28). For in the prophet Micah it is written in this way: The Lord shall go forth from His place, and shall come down and tread upon the high places of the earth, and the minds under it shall be consumed, and the valleys shall be cleft (Micah 1:3). Also in Isaiah: The Lord of hosts shall go forth and crush war, and will stir up the heavens, and will cry out over His enemies with strength (Isa. 42:13). Therefore, God will go forth from His place when He is compelled to break His rest and gentleness and mercy for the correction of sinners, who, though by nature He is sweet, becomes bitter through our fault, not to Himself, but to those who endure, for whom the torments are bitter. Concerning His nature, He Himself speaks otherwise through the prophet, saying: I am God and I do not change (Mal. 3:6). Therefore, it is also said through James: With whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration (James 1:17). Therefore Paul also says of Christ: Who is the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15). And again: Now to the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God (1 Tim. 1:17). And in the Gospel it is written: No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him (Jn. 1:18).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For by the wondrous works of the almighty God the faithful are instructed to beware of involving themselves in the sins of the wicked, and rather to strive to keep themselves untainted by such matters, and by maintaining faith and hope in the Lord, not to neglect the time granted to them for doing penance and good works; indeed, with all their strength, through love, they should try to serve their Creator.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The book of Exodus narrates how the Lord, through Moses and Aaron, struck the Egyptians, namely, the enemies of God’s people with ten plagues, and at times allowed them to breathe amidst these plagues, so that, having been chastised, they might be corrected. But because they persisted in wickedness, they were destroyed by divine vengeance. On the other hand, the people of God, to whom the promise was made and to their fathers, were scarcely chastised and partly comforted, as long as they endured to be educated by discipline. However, after they spurned the Gospel of Christ and crucified the Son of God, they were, in a wondrous manner, turned from friends into enemies, and therefore expelled from their own land, dispersed throughout the whole world, and finally felt harshly chastised, which previously they refused to understand when corrected by paternal kindness. We can similarly interpret this sentiment regarding the martyrs of Christ and their persecutors, because when those persecutors tortured the confessors of Christ with torments, they could, if they wished, be instructed by their patience to abandon the worship of idols and submit themselves to the Christian religion. But just as the martyrs attained eternal glory through temporal sufferings, so too did the persecutors, after the brief joys of this life, sink into eternal punishments.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This is what is written in the psalm: Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord (Ps. 32:10). For there is a great difference between the judgment of the elect and that of the depraved, because the Lord corrects the former to cleanse them from sins and restrain them from vices, but the latter so that they may pay the penalties for their pride and treachery, and recognize that they cannot resist the ruler of all. Indeed, happy is he who always keeps before his eyes the compassion and goodness of his judge when judging, and just as he wishes the Lord to have mercy on him, so he should not refuse to have mercy on others, because judgment will be without mercy for him who does not show mercy. For blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matt. 5:7).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The punishment for those who lived unjustly and senselessly in their lives was that, through the things they worshipped, they endured torment; and by divine judgment, since they were unwilling to know their Creator and to honor Him as was fitting, they were handed over to a depraved mind, to do those things which are not fitting, dishonoring their bodies among themselves, so that in this they would have shame now, and in the future, eternal torment. The apostle Paul explains the truth of this matter in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is evident in them. For God has shown it to them. For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made: even His eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse; because, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor were thankful, but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things. Therefore God gave them up to the lusts of their own hearts, to uncleanness, to dishonor their own bodies among themselves, who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen (Rom. 1:18-25). Therefore their heart was blinded, so that the majesty of the invisible God, whom they had recognized from these works, they changed, not to men, but, what is worse, into an inexcusable crime, into the likeness of men, so that God is called by them in the form of corruptible man, that is, the image of a man; so that those whom they do not dare to call by the name of God while alive, they receive the images of the dead into the glory of God. How great is the sickness, how great the foolishness, to call these wise to their own damnation, among whom the dead have more power than the living, and the dead are preferred to the living; for, departing from the living God, they favor the dead, of whom it is written, “A mortal man makes a dead thing with wicked hands” (Wis. 15:17); for therefore they diminished the majesty and glory of God, that to these things which are least and smallest, they gave the honor due to God’s likeness. For the Babylonians were the first to call a thing god, the image of Bel, once a dead man, who is said to have ruled over them. They also worshipped the serpent, the dragon, which Daniel, the man of God, killed, whose likeness they have. The Egyptians, however, worshipped a four-footed animal, which they called Apis, in the likeness of a cow. Jeroboam imitated this evil, making calves in Samaria for the Jews to sacrifice to, and birds, because the pagans have sacred rites for ravens. Yet the Egyptians worshipped the images of all these things I have mentioned, and others which it is not necessary to mention now. These things were done by those who considered themselves wise in the world; for, because they did not honor the invisible God by doing these things, neither could they rightly understand the things that are visible.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Indeed, those who, having been chastised by the scourges of God, were not corrected, have experienced the fitting punishment of damnation; for God chastises for this purpose, that He may amend, not wishing anyone to perish, because He wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. But he who is ungrateful for God's visitation, and through impatience falls into murmuring, is led from temporal chastisement to perpetual torments.
Against Marivadus the Arian, PL 62

We prove that the Son is true, as the Father is, by the words of the prophets and the Gospels, Isaiah saying: To those serving me there shall be called a new name, which shall be blessed upon the earth; and they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God (Isa. 65:15). And in Solomon: Those whom they think to be gods shall fear, by whom they shall be destroyed; seeing him whom they once denied, they have acknowledged as the true God (Wis. 12:27).

Wretched breeding, which for so long served idols, was also deceived by error and believed those to be gods by whose persuasions they were led astray, and because of this they were subjected to various punishments. Therefore, many from among them later recognized the true God, whom previously they refused to believe in through His benefits, as almighty in just judgment. For He could not remain hidden, since He is acknowledged to be the ruler of all, because either He grants mercy here to those who are converted through repentance, or He assigns everlasting punishment in the future to those who rebel through pride.

(Haydock) --- In this and the three following chapters, the miseries of idolatry are described, to shew the value of wisdom and piety. (Calmet) --- Without the knowledge of God, all is darkness, 1 Corinthians ii. 2. (St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho) --- Is. He who is, must be the most proper name of God, Exodus iii. 14. Philosophers could perceive that all creatures had a beginning, and that there must be some first cause or God, whom some confessed, but did not honour as they ought, Romans i. (Worthington) --- Could not. Inasmuch as they were vain. (Haydock)

Fire. The chief god of the Persians. --- Wind. Zephyrus, &c. --- Air. Which is perhaps the wind. Socrates was accused of adoring nothing, but heaven and the clouds, (Aristot.[Aristotle?] nub.) as the Jews were. Nil præter nubes et Cœli numen adorant. (Juvenal xiv. 97.) --- Stars. The zodiac, or pleiads. This species of idolatry was most ancient and general. --- Water. The ocean, Neptune, &c. The Egyptians adored water above all, as the origin of other things. Hence they were punished first by it. (Philo, vit. Mor. 1.) --- Moon. These were mostly the objects of worship, under the names of Baal, Astarte, (Calmet) the Phœbus, or Dianæ of the Romans. (Haydock)

Thereby. God is announced by the heavens, and by all creatures, Psalm xviii. 1., and Romans i. 20. "Who can look up to heaven, and be so foolish as not to allow that there is a God?" (Cicero, Harusp.)

Of men. The pagans in general took the material statue to be the residence of a god. (St. Augustine, City of God chap. vii. 6., and viii. 13.) --- The more learned regarded the figures of the sun, &c., as his representations, while others supposed that Jupiter meant the heavens, Juno the air, Vulcan, fire, &c. --- Hand. This is to abuse antiquity. The idol of the Arabs was a rough stone. In more polished nations, the workmanship of Praxiteles, Phidias, &c., was more regarded. (Calmet) --- As no creature deserves to be esteemed a god, much less do the works of men's hands. (Worthington)

Vermilion. The ancients greatly esteemed this colour, (Calmet) and painted with it the statues of their gods on festival days, and the bodies of those who had the honour of a triumph. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xxxiii. 6.)

Iron. Baruch (vi. 26.) ridicules the same custom, and the other prophets intimate that the pagans took these statues to be really gods, otherwise their practice was no more blameable than that of the Jews, who fastened the cherubim to the ark with gold, and carried them. But the latter did not believe that the Deity resided personally in those images; no more than we do, that Christ is attached to his image on the cross. This distinguishes the behaviour of the faithful from that of pagans. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For all men by nature were vain, in whom there was ignorance of God. And if every living man is altogether vain, how much more vain are those who do not acknowledge their Creator. But all men are vain in whom there is no knowledge of God, that is, the fear and reverence of God. Therefore it is said through Job: Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding (Job 28:28). For he departs from evil who withdraws from the worship of idols; he fears God who keeps His commandments. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; a good understanding have all they that do His commandments (Ps. 111:10). and who were unable from the visible good things to know him who is. For from good works they could have known the good craftsman, who truly is, because He is always unchallengeable, who alone has immortality, and dwells in inaccessible light; who is always the same, and whose years never fail: who is eternal and omnipotent, without beginning and without end, always remaining in Himself, according to His will governs and directs all things; therefore, the vanity of men is most vain, who worship creatures instead of the Creator.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For some worshipped fire as a divine power, which they called Vulcan; others worshipped the ether or air, which they named Jupiter or Juno; others worshipped excessive water, which they called Neptune; others the circle of stars, who distributed the positions and courses of the stars according to the various shapes of animals; others venerated the sun as God, which they called Phoebus or Apollo; others the moon, which they used to call Diana. For, deceived by such error, they attributed the power of the almighty God to their false inventions, as a certain pagan poet concluded in three verses, saying: "So many and such images did God place in the heavens, and through the dark shadows scattered, He commanded the bright lights to give clarity to the devastating night." But if it is not possible for the stars to be gods, then neither can the sun nor the moon be gods, since they differ from the lights of the stars not in kind, but in size. But if these are not gods, then neither is the sky, in which all these are contained. In the same way, if the earth which we tread, which we cultivate and till for sustenance, is not a god, then neither will the fields nor the mountains be gods; if these are not gods, then the whole earth cannot be considered a god. Likewise, if the water which serves living beings for drinking or washing is not a god, then neither are the springs from which water flows. If the springs are not gods, then neither are the rivers which are gathered from the springs. If the rivers also are not gods, then the sea, which is made up of rivers, cannot be considered a god. But if neither the sky, nor the earth, nor the sea, which are parts of the world, can be gods, then neither is the whole world a god, which the same Stoics claim to be both living and wise, and therefore God, in which they have been so inconsistent that nothing has been said by them which has not also been overturned by themselves.
Augustine of Hippo, Sermon 141.1-3

That God is a certain eternal life, unchangeable, intelligible, understanding, wise, making others wise, even some philosophers of this age have seen. They have indeed seen a fixed, stable, unchanging truth, where all the reasons for all created things are found, but they saw it from afar; they saw it, but while in error; and therefore, to that great, indescribable, and beatifying possession, they did not find the way by which one might arrive. For since they too saw (as much as can be seen by a human) the Creator through the creation, the Maker through the thing made, the Fashioner of the world through the world, the Apostle Paul is a witness, whom Christians ought surely to believe. For he says, when speaking of such people: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. These, as you recognize, are the words of the Apostle Paul. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness. Did he say they do not hold the truth? Rather: they hold the truth in unrighteousness. What they hold is good; but where they hold it is evil. They hold the truth in unrighteousness. But it might be asked: How do those ungodly ones hold the truth? Did God speak to any of them? Did they receive the law, as the people of Israel did through Moses? Whence then do they hold the truth, even in unrighteousness? Listen to what follows, and it is shown. Because what is known of God, he says, is manifest in them; for God has shown it to them. Did he show it to those to whom he did not give the law? Hear how he showed it. For his invisible things, being understood by the things that are made, are clearly seen. Question the world, the beauty of the sky, the brightness and arrangement of the stars, the sun sufficient for the day, the moon the comfort of the night; question the earth, fruitful with herbs and trees, full of animals, adorned with humans; question the sea, full of so many and such kinds of creatures that swim; question the air, enlivened by so many birds; question all things, and see if by their own sense they do not answer you: God made us. These things even noble philosophers sought, and from the art they recognized the artist. What then? Why is the wrath of God revealed against that ungodliness? Because they hold the truth in unrighteousness? Let him come, let him show how. For he has already said how they knew. His invisible things, that is, of God, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made; even his eternal power and divinity; so that they are without excuse. Because, when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor gave thanks; but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. These are the words of the Apostle, not mine: And their foolish heart was darkened; for, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. What they found by curiosity, they lost by pride. Professing themselves to be wise, that is, attributing to themselves the gift of God, they became fools. The words, I say, are the Apostle's: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. Show, prove their foolishness. Show, Apostle, and just as you showed us how they could come to the knowledge of God, because his invisible things, being understood by the things that are made, are clearly seen; so now show how, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. Listen: Because, he says, they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things. For the pagans made for themselves gods in the forms of these animals. You found God, and you worship an idol. You found the truth, and you hold that very truth in unrighteousness. And what you knew through the works of God, you lose through the works of man. You considered everything; you gathered the order of heaven, earth, sea, and all the elements; but you do not wish to consider this, that the world is the work of God, the idol is the work of the craftsman. If the craftsman, as he gave the idol its shape, also gave it a heart, the craftsman would be worshipped by the idol itself.
SERMON 384:1.1

The prophet says, "I will be filled with the revelation of his glory." We can sing of the glory that awaits us, of the goods that will accompany it, of the splendor with which it will shine, but we are incapable of expressing all of this in words. Paul explains the reason for this when he writes, "Those things that eye has not seen, that ear has not heard and that have never entered the heart of human beings, God has prepared for those who love him." These many eternal, heavenly gifts have been prepared by the almighty Lord for his faithful, holy people throughout the world. But who is God, who has arranged all these things for us? Of him we say only that we do not know how to measure or express or understand him, that he is beyond all, outside of all, above all. He surpasses all his creatures; he is beyond his works, above all of them. I could try to express his greatness, but he is greater, or his beauty, but he is more beautiful. He is sweeter than every sweetness, brighter than every splendor, more just than all justice, stronger than all strength, gentler than all gentleness. Reason does not admit of the creature claiming equality with its Creator, nor that something produced is put on the level of the one who produced it. Precisely thus we read in the prophet, "The one who made powerful things is more powerful than they are. And the one who made beautiful things is more beautiful than they."
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It would have been fitting that the most beautiful and splendid Creator be recognized through beautiful creatures, but they became vain in their thoughts and chose to serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Therefore, they are refuted not only by the truth but also by their own words; for just as a house, made for the purpose of dwelling, feels nothing of itself and is subject to the master who made or inhabits it, so the world, feeling nothing of itself, is subject to God the Maker, who made it for His own use. Therefore, the sinner is at fault before the foolish for two reasons: first, because they prefer the elements, that is, the works of God, to God Himself; then, because they worship images of the elements themselves, fashioned in human form, for they make images of the sun and moon in the manner of humans, likewise of fire and earth and sea, which they call Vulcan, Vesta, and Neptune. Such is the desire of men for images that they are even more attracted to those which are rare; they delight, of course, in gold and gems and ivory, the beauty and brilliance of these dazzle their eyes, nor do they consider any place sacred unless these things have shone there. Therefore, under the hoax of gods, greed and desire are worshipped; for they believe that the gods love whatever they themselves desire, whatever it is for which thefts, murders, and robberies are daily committed, and for which wars overturn peoples and cities throughout the world. Therefore, they consecrate to the gods their spoils and plunder, whom, indeed, they must admit to be weak and devoid of the highest virtue, if they are subject to desires: for why should we think them heavenly, if they desire something from the earth? Or blessed, if they need anything? Or incorruptible, if they take pleasure in those things in the desire for which human greed is rightly condemned?
Catechetical Lecture 9:2

If it is not possible to see the divine nature with eyes of flesh, it is possible to gain an image of the divine power of the Creator from his works. Solomon says this: "In fact, one knows the author by analogy from the greatness and beauty of creatures." He does not say simply that one knows the author from creatures but adds "by analogy." The more we consider his creatures in a contemplative way, in fact, the more God will show himself to be great. And the more our heart is raised in contemplation, the higher will be the image that we have of God.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Paul the Apostle, writing to the Romans in his Epistle, as we have already shown above, expressed the likeness of this place, saying: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because that which is known of God is revealed in them, for God has revealed it to them. For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse (Rom. 1:18-20). The knowledge of God is revealed from the structure of the world. For God, who is by nature invisible, can also be known as visible, for a work was made by him which, by its visibility, reveals the maker, so that through the certain, the uncertain can be known; so that by what is impossible for others, he who made this work might be believed to be the God of all; so that they are without excuse: because they could not be ignorant of his existence and his working for their benefit, for it is clear to all that he has ordained those things which are produced for human use in the course of the year; but when they had known him, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their imaginations, claiming to be wise, they became fools (Rom. 1:21-22). For they consider themselves wise because they think they are investigating physical principles, examining the course of the stars and the qualities of the elements, but despising the Lord of these things, they are therefore fools. Since these things are praiseworthy, how much more so is their creator? Yet, having suffered the shame of neglecting God, they often use a miserable excuse, saying that through these things one can go to God, just as one reaches the king through companions. Come now, is anyone so senseless or so forgetful of his own salvation as to give the honor of the king to a companion, when, if anyone is found even to discuss such a thing, he is rightly condemned for treason? And these people do not consider themselves guilty who prefer the honor of God's name to the creature, and, leaving the Lord, worship fellow servants, as if there were something more that could be preserved for God! For indeed, it is through the king that one goes to tribunes or companions, because the king is, after all, a man, and does not know to whom he should entrust the state; but to God, whom nothing escapes, for he knows the merits of all, there is no need for an intercessor to obtain favor, but only a devoted mind.
SERMON 68:4

"If they were capable of sufficient knowledge to account for the universe, how is it that they did not more easily find its Lord?" They are blamed for having spent their time, their activity and their discussions scrutinizing, and in a certain way measuring, what is created. They investigated the movement of the planets, the distance between the stars, the course of the heavenly bodies. Through these studies, they arrived at such a scientific knowledge as to be able to predict eclipses of the sun and the moon, which then occurred on the day and hour predicted, for the length of time and at the exact point in space they had said. What ability! What capacity! But when they were at the point of seeking to know the Creator—who was not far from them—they were unable to find him. If they had found him, they would have had him in themselves.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

They therefore come to the gods, not so much for the sake of religion, which can have no place in things ill-prepared and perishable, as to feast their eyes on gold, to gaze at the polish of refined marble or ivory, to handle with greedy contemplation the garments distinguished by little stones and colors, or cups adorned with shining gems; and the more decorative and beautiful the temples and statues are, the more majesty they are believed to possess. Therefore, their religion is nothing other than what their desire admires. We have often said that silver and gold can be understood as speech and thought, which, since they are given by God to humans so that they may either speak or think of God and praise their Creator, they misuse this gift in the imitation of idols, according to what is written: I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal from my silver and gold (Hosea 2:8). Therefore, when someone, terrified by the fear of the Lord, first hides idols in the cave of his heart and, not daring to bring forth what he has wrongly fashioned, conceals them in the depths of the earth, the next step is to cast away what was previously engraved and not allow it to remain in himself, according to that saying of Isaiah: On that day, a man will cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats. And they will enter into the clefts of the rocks and into the caves of the stones from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth (Isa. 2:20-21).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This wisdom was brought forth to insult idols and idolaters, so that such makers and worshippers might understand how wicked and how close to eternal death it is to abandon the one omnipotent God and Creator of all things, and to worship various creations as divinity in contempt of God. Therefore, through the prophet, the Lord spoke long ago to His people about His own veneration and the falsity of idols: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no other God. Who is like me? Let him call and declare, and set in order for me since I established the ancient people, and let him announce to them the things to come. Do not fear, nor be troubled; from then on I have made you hear, and I have announced the future: you are my witnesses. Is there any God besides me, or a maker whom I do not know? All makers of idols are nothing, and their most beloved things will not profit them: they themselves are their witnesses, because they do not see nor understand, so that they may be confused. Who has formed a god, or cast a graven image that is of no use? Behold, all his associates shall be confused; for they are craftsmen, and they gather from all, all shall stand and tremble and be confounded together. The ironworker works with a file in the coals, and with hammers he shapes it, and works with the strength of his arm; he will hunger and grow weak, he will not drink water and will faint. The woodworker stretches a line and shapes it with a plane; he makes it with a square, and turns it with a compass: and he makes the image of a man, as a beautiful person dwelling in a house. He cuts down cedars, takes holm oak and oak which stood among the trees of the forest; he plants a pine which the rain nourished, and it becomes fuel for men; he takes some of it and is warmed, and kindles it and bakes bread; but from the rest he makes a god, and worships it; he makes a graven image, and bows down before it. He burns half of it in the fire, and with the half he eats meat; he cooks stew and is satisfied, and is warmed, and says: Aha, I am warmed, I have seen the fire. But the rest of it he makes into a god, and a graven image for himself; he bows down before it, and worships it, and prays saying: Deliver me, for you are my god. They did not know nor understand; for their eyes are blinded so that they may not see, nor understand with their heart. Nor do they consider in their mind, nor know, nor feel, so as to say: I burned half of it in the fire, and baked bread on its coals, cooked meat and ate, and from the rest shall I make an idol? Shall I bow down before a block of wood? Part of it is ashes: a foolish heart has worshipped it, and has not delivered his soul, nor said: Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand (Isa. 44:6-20)? The sense of this prophecy's narrative is as follows: For when it says: I am the first and the last, it is the same as what is elsewhere read as spoken from divine majesty: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end (Rev. 21:6). For He does not say He is alone, but that besides His power and wisdom there is no external God, condemning the opinion of many gods and their images: Who, He says, is like me? Let him call things that are not as if they are, and explain the order of my creation by which I have freed all things with reason, since I made man upon the earth, and not only do I will, but I also seek knowledge of the future. Therefore you, Israel, whose king and redeemer I am, do not fear images, which you learned to be nothing on Mount Sinai. Is perhaps another creator whom I do not know, or besides this is there another world which shows the power of an unknown God? Nor are only the things made, but also those who make them considered as nothing: and when the time of vengeance comes, the works of their hands will by no means be able to deliver them, which blind and insensible things confound their makers. For who can believe that a god is formed by a file, drill, and hammer, or that images are cast in coals, or that by a line, plane, and compass they suddenly arise as gods, especially when the poverty of the craftsman's art is shown by hunger and thirst: for a wooden statue is made expressing the human form, and the more beautiful it is, the more it is thought to be an imposing god, and it is placed in a temple and enclosed in an eternal prison, which grew for a long time in the forests, and according to the variety of trees was a cedar, holm oak, oak tree, or pine, and in a wondrous manner its segments and shavings are thrown into the fire to warm the maker of the god and cook various stews; but the other part is shaped into a god so that, when the work is completed, its maker worships it and implores help from his own work, nor does he understand or consider, indeed neither flesh nor mind sees with eyes, that it cannot be a god whose part has been consumed by fire, nor can divine majesty be made by the hand of man, and the prophetic word is more fully woven about the mockery of idols, which are easy to understand and do not desire a patchwork or even extra exposition. On which Flaccus also writes in satire, mocking the images of the pagans. "Once I was a fig tree trunk, a useless piece of wood, When a carpenter, unsure whether to make a bench or a Priapus, Preferred to make a god. Therefore I am a god, the greatest fear of thieves and birds." But whatever has been said about idols can also be applied to the leaders of heresies, who construct and venerate images of their doctrines with cunning hearts, knowing that what they have made is a simulation; nor is their own error sufficient for them unless they have deceived the simple from prayer, and those who think that godliness is a means of gain, and who devour widows' houses, abusing the ignorance of the common people. In this way, with dialectical skill, as with a well-turned axe, file, and plane, they shape their god, and hammer him out, and make golden him with the charm of rhetorical speech, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame.
Augustine of Hippo, Sermon 105.12-13

The gods of gold, of wood, are as regards their costliness unequal; but as to "having eyes, and seeing not," they are equal. See to what sort of guardians learned men have entrusted Rome, to those "who have eyes, and see not." Or if they were able to preserve Rome, why did they first perish themselves? They say: "Rome perished at the same time." Nevertheless they perished. "No," they say, "they did not perish themselves, but their statues." Well, how then could they keep your houses, who were not able to keep their own statues? Alexandria once lost such gods as these. Constantinople some time since, ever since it was made a grand city, for it was made so by a Christian Emperor, lost its false gods; and yet it has increased, and still increases, and remains. And remain it will, as long as God pleases. For we do not to this city either promise an eternal duration because we say this. Carthage remains now in its possession of the Name of Christ, yet once on a time its goddess Caelestis was overthrown; because celestial she was not, but terrestrial. And that which they say is not true, that immediately on losing her gods Rome has been taken and ruined. It is not true at all; their images were overthrown before; and even so were the Goths with Rhadagaisus conquered.

n: Him. The folly of exposing one's life, without necessity, to such imminent danger at sea, is great; though much less than to confide in idols, (Calmet) which are commonly made of more corruptible wood than ships. (Worthington)

Waves. Of the Red sea, (Vatable) through which the Israelites passed, (Worthington) or rather hast taught navigation to Noe[Noah], (ver. 6.) and enabled him to build the finest vessel that ever appeared.
Saved. Before the invention of the compass, long voyages were deemed the effects of rashness, or of great confidence in Providence. (Calmet)

Cometh. By which Noe[Noah] was preserved, (Cornelius a Lapide) or criminals are executed. (Jansenius) --- The author foretells the redemption of mankind on the cross. (Worthington) (Galatians iii. 13.) (St. Augustine, City of God chap. xv. 26; St. Ambrose, Psalm cxviii. ser. 8.)

Fornication. Invention of idols brought people to give way to spiritual fornication, and corruption of manners. (Worthington) --- They freely practised what was sanctioned by the example of their gods. (St. Augustine, City of God ii. 7., and 3 Kings xiv. 24., and 4 Kings xxiii. 7, 3.) (Calmet)

Beginning. Truth is always prior to falsehood. (Haydock) --- Josephus (Jewish Antiquities i. 4.) says, idolatry commenced in the 8th generation, and the Jews assert, under Enos. "Then began the name of God to be profaned," as the Chaldean, &c., translate, Genesis iv. 26. (St. Jerome, q. Heb.) --- The corruption of morals was the natural consequence, ver. 12. --- Ever. Christ shall destroy them. (Calmet)

Servants. This was at first done privately, and made the way for public idolatry. Calvin attempts to refute this assertion, maintaining that Laban's idols were more ancient, and not images. But this argument is nugatory, as theraphim may be rendered either images, (Protestants, 1552.) or idols. (Protestants, 1603.) The latter version is preferable, as Laban called them his gods, and the Greek and Latin have idols. It is also certain, that Ninus set up the image of his father, Jupiter Belus, to be honoured by the people, before Abraham's time; and the fathers agree, that the making of images in memory of the dead, was the first occasion of idolatry. (St. Chrysostom, hom. 87. in Matthew; St. Jerome in Osee ii., &c.) (Worthington) --- Nimrod ordered divine honours to be paid to his deceased son. (Gul. Paris. Leg.) --- Yet this fact is not certain. Diophante, the Lacedemonian, assigns the same origin to idolatry as is here given. (Grotius)

Ignorant. The arts of sculpture and painting may be prejudicial, (Calmet) and were therefore banished by Moses from his republic, (Philo) as the Jews were so prone to idolatry, chap. xv. 4. The case is different with us. (Haydock)
Name. It cannot with propriety be given to any but God. (Worthington) --- The Jews explain this of the name Jehovah, which they will never pronounce. (Calmet)

Children. This was done by the Chanaanites, Hebrews, &c., chap. xii. 23., and Isaias lvii. 5. --- Hidden. The sacrifices of Ceres, Bacchus, &c., were performed in the dark, and horrible impurities were committed, Ephesians v. 12. --- Madness. Before they be initiated in the mysteries of Ceres, or prostitute themselves in honour of the deities of impurity, (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities xviii. 4.) in the very temples. Quo non prostrat femina templo? (Juvenal ix.) (Calmet) --- Many crimes proceed from idolatry. (Worthington)

Mad. Like the Bacchanalian women, running crowned with serpents, and eating raw flesh. --- Lies. The delusions of the devil, or the fraud of priests. --- Easily. Those who believe not in religion, or in the power of him by whom they swear, can give no security by an oath. They fear no harm, ver. 29. Yet they are perjured if they believe Jupiter, for example, to be a god, (St. Augustine, ep. 54. ad Pub.) and if they do not, they are impious; abusing an oath, which is in itself sacred. (Calmet)

Just. Literally, "the punishment of sinners always walketh about," &c. (Haydock) --- "The stone does not hear thee speaking, but God punishes the deceiver." (St. Augustine) --- The pagans supposed that their idols sometimes punished perjury. (Juvenal, Sat. viii.) --- It is God who does it. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He likewise presents these things, just as the previous ones, as a reproach against idolaters, because it is the greatest folly that a man, created in the image of God, possessing a rational soul from Him, by which he was able to devise the art of how to have a way to travel on the waves, building a ship according to his skill in the craft, does not give honor to Him who gave him this knowledge, but rather invokes an idol which he himself has fashioned with similar skill but even greater vanity. For since he is greater and better by reason of nature than the insensible thing which he himself has shaped into some image, he ought not to have erred so that the greater worships the lesser, because the lesser ought to seek help from the greater, not the greater from the lesser. Moreover, by divine gift, just as the preparation of the ship, so also the course of sailing must be sought, because the Almighty Creator destroys whomever He abandons; but whoever is guided by Him exults in complete prosperity. But all heretics who, in their doctrines, establish various images of errors, are therefore engulfed in the waves of this world, because they have abandoned the ship of the Church and did not wish to have God as their guide.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, according to the history, the power of the Lord was demonstrated when He made the people of Israel cross the Red Sea on dry foot; likewise, when they left the desert, He led them through the bed of the Jordan, with the waters divided on either side, so as to instill terror in the nations of the Canaanites to be exterminated. But according to the allegory, the Lord Himself prepares for His faithful a path of faith and constancy amid the waves of the world and the torments of persecutors, through which they can pass unharmed from every scandal, nor will they need human comfort there, where the power of the Most High shows the marvelous effects of His virtue.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The wondrous Creator gave knowledge to His creature, so that in the present age he might be able to attend to his own necessity, and serve the will of his Lord. Therefore also from the beginning, when the human race began to serve idolatry, and all evils were fashioned upon the earth by proud giants, the almighty Judge commanded His faithful servant Noah to build an ark, through which he and his offspring might be saved, and the species of all living creatures might be preserved for the future restoration of the world. The mystery of this, indeed, the Apostle Peter shows in his Epistle, saying: Christ once died for our sins, the just for the unjust, that He might offer us to God; put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit. In which also He went and preached to the spirits in prison, who had once been disobedient, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water; which now saves you also, baptism of a like figure (1 Peter 3:18-21). They say that the form of baptism is likened to the ark and the waters of the flood, and rightly so, because the very construction of the ark from smoothed wood signifies the building of the Church, which is made from the gathering of the souls of the faithful by the architects of the Word. And that, when the whole world perished, only a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water, signifies that, in comparison to the perishing Gentiles, Jews, heretics, and false believers, the number of the elect is much smaller. Therefore, concerning the narrow gate and the strait way which leads to life, it is said: And few there are who find it (Matt. 7:13-14). And again: Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32). Therefore, that the water of the flood did not save those outside the ark, but destroyed them, undoubtedly prefigured that every heretic, although having the sacrament of baptism, is not raised by the waters but is drowned by them into hell, while the ark is lifted up to heaven. Also, the very number eight of the souls who were saved through water signifies that the holy Church receives the washing of baptism as a sacrament of the Lord's resurrection, so that just as He rose from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we, cleansed from sins by the water of regeneration, may walk in newness of life.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This comparison of the two trees is different, because one deserves blessing, while the other deserves a curse.
