For blessed is the wood of the cross, on which, through the blood of Christ, the world was restored, and the redemption of the human race was perfected. On the contrary, the idol is cursed, that is, the image and worship of false gods, whose destruction is certain, and eternal torment awaits its maker. For the Devil will rightly be punished for having persuaded and agreed to have divine honor offered to himself; and men who worshipped him as God will deservedly suffer torments, because they tried to venerate falsehood instead of truth, and the creature instead of the Creator. But since we often find in the Holy Scriptures that wood is set for man, according to the rule of figurative speech, blessed is the man who speaks words of truth and does works of righteousness. But the heretic who worships the inventions of his own error is cursed, and assigned to eternal destruction, he himself, indeed, and his work, that is, his doctrine, which he presumed to teach falsely as truth.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, it is also said through Jeremiah: Every man has become foolish by his own knowledge, every maker of idols is confounded by his carved image, because his molten image is false, and there is no spirit in them; for their works are vain and worthy of ridicule; in the time of their visitation, they shall perish (Jer. 10:14-15).
Sermon 360A

In the book of Wisdom, it is written thus: Therefore there shall be a regard even for the idols of the nations. For God did not look for a long time on the idols that were worshipped for a long time, and on the sacrifices made to idols. He who always sees, at some point condescends to look. He saw with patience, he regarded with vengeance. He says there shall be a regard for the idols of the nations, because they were made from God's creations to incite hatred. For they provoke God with the creations of God. How do they provoke God with the creations? For a craftsman made a god, but God made wood. A goldsmith made an idol, but God made gold. Why do you make out of his creation something that he would detest; out of God's creation, you shape something that he would detest? You should shape well what he would love. You want to put your own image in wood, take the image of God into yourself. Why do you erase inwardly and carve outwardly? He says, the creations of God were made to provoke hatred, and as trials for the souls of men, and as a snare for the feet of the foolish. For the beginning of fornication is the seeking of idols. If a woman having many husbands is praised, let also the soul worshipping many gods be praised. If a woman is an adulteress through true husbands, how much more is a soul through false gods? For the beginning of fornication is the seeking of idols, and their invention is the corruption of life.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the idols of the nations are not gods, and their inhabitants are, evidently, evil spirits, deserving of pardon, since men who were created in the image and honor of God were being led away from their Creator, and by casting them into the snare of their own error, were being overthrown. Likewise, if heretics persist in their wickedness, by which they lead men from truth into falsehood, and do not correct themselves and do penance, they will not escape the judgment of eternal fire.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Although there are many kinds of fornication, the worst is that by which the soul fornicates, departing from God and worshipping idols. Similarly, that is also destructive which abandons the truth of divine doctrine and follows the falsehood of heretical opinion. For the Apostle Paul calls greed the service of idols (Eph. 5:5), from which it can be assumed that every evil desire may rightly be called fornication, when the soul, neglecting the higher law by which the lower is governed, is corrupted as if prostituted for a price to the base will of the natures. But all these things, just as they were not created from the beginning, so also they will not remain forever. For the Lord will destroy all deceitful lips, and will cut off all who speak lies (Ps. 12:3). Therefore, it is also said through Jeremiah: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth will perish from the earth and from under these heavens. But the Lord is the true God, he is the living God and the eternal King (Jer. 10:10-11). Therefore idols first arose, the following sentence shows.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

However, Firmianus Lactantius, in the first book he wrote on the false religion of the gods, presents similar things regarding this passage, saying: It is not obscure by what reasoning men began to be called gods, for it was because of the depravity of men who lived a rural life without any ruler. There is no doubt that in those times they began to praise a man who was king, and his whole people, with the highest praises, so that they even called them gods, whether they truly believed this because of the miracle of virtue, being still rude and simple, or, as often happens, out of flattery for present power, or because of the benefits by which they were brought to civilization. Then, when these kings were dear to them, they also arranged their lives accordingly, and after their death left behind a great longing for themselves. Therefore, men fashioned images of them, so that they might have some consolation from the contemplation of their likenesses, and, going further out of love, they began to honor the memory of the deceased, so that they might seem both to repay gratitude to those who had deserved well, and to attract their successors to the desire of ruling well. Cicero teaches this about the nature of the gods, saying: But the common custom of men has taken up the practice that those who excel in benefits, men, are raised to heaven by fame and will. Therefore Hercules, later Castor, therefore Pollux, later Aesculapius, therefore Liber. And in another place: And in most cities it can be understood that, for the sake of sharpening virtue, or because they would more willingly face danger for the sake of the republic, the memory of the best and bravest men was consecrated in honor of the immortal gods. By this reasoning, of course, the Romans consecrated their Caesars, and the Moors their kings; therefore, little by little, religions began to exist, while those first who knew them in that rite filled their children and grandchildren, and then all their descendants; and yet these greatest kings, because of the fame of their name, were worshipped in all provinces. But privately, each people venerated with the highest reverence the founders of their race or city, or men notable for their bravery, or women remarkable for their chastity, as the Egyptians did Isis, the Carthaginians Urania, the Romans Quirinus, Samos Juno, Naxos Liber, the Moors Juba, the Latins Faunus; likewise, Paphos Venus, Delos Apollo, the Macedonians Scabrius, the Athenians Minerva, Lemnos Vulcan; therefore, throughout peoples and regions, various sacred rites were undertaken, while men desired to show gratitude to their rulers. And why they should bestow other honors on those who lack life, I cannot find: therefore, the devotion of those who succeeded contributed greatly to the error, who, so that they might seem born of divine stock, bestowed divine honors on their parents, and ordered them to be bestowed. Therefore, he says, the incommunicable name was placed upon stones and wood: because the incomprehensible name of the living and omnipotent God, who alone is, they wickedly ascribed to images treacherously composed of insensible and fragile matter, and, together with false religion, shamelessly destroyed themselves with all vices.
SERMONS 26:28

Human beings seek purification, but the devil, proud spirit, seeing that they sought this out of pride and boasted of it, anticipated them and presented himself as a mediator, capable of giving a semblance of purity to their souls. In this, hinting at his pride, he led people to think that he was necessary, that is, to show them that a soul desirous to reach God could purify itself through recourse to magic arts. He thus instituted in the temples those sacrilegious rites that assure purification to those who perform them. Many of those images were in fact suggested, as the Scripture says, by the desire to honor certain people held to be great, people not present or dead people.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and serpents, and they exchanged the truth of God for a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever; although they called themselves wise, they became fools: for they were given over to a reprobate mind, so that they dishonored their bodies among themselves, and those who refused to enter into a covenant with God through right faith and good works, being placed under the worship of the Devil, could in no way have true peace among themselves. Therefore they sacrificed their own children, as the pagans themselves did in the rites of Saturn, who sacrificed to Saturn out of hatred for Jupiter, and extinguished tender and innocent souls, which is the age most sweet to parents, without any regard for virtue. Others, indeed, offered human blood to the virtue they called Bellona; for the priests themselves sacrificed not with another's blood, but with their own, striking themselves with drawn swords. About this, Quintilian rightly says: "If God requires this, He is angry." Others, performing obscure rites, held vigils full of madness, as they were accustomed to do in the rites of Egyptian Isis and Eleusinian Ceres; for just as Osiris was sought there with the lamentation of his mother, so here Proserpina, abducted for the incestuous marriage of her uncle, was sought. Because Ceres is said to have searched for her in Sicily with torches lit from the summit of Etna, therefore her rites are celebrated with the tossing of burning torches. Likewise, in the rites of Father Liber, vigils full of madness were held; also in the festival of the Great Mother, where, following the example of their gods, who spent the night in feasting and games during her festival, these people consumed the whole night in useless play. Neither life nor marriage was kept pure by the pagans themselves, because they thought they could please their gods through lust and impurities of life; for all things were confused where reason and true religion held no place, but the more wicked someone was, the more he thought he pleased his god.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

There is no greater madness than to abandon the living God and serve dead idols, and therefore the cause and beginning of all evil is the worship of idols, because after the human mind turns away from its creator, it becomes entangled in the errors of all crimes. For the beginning of all sin is pride (Eccles. 10:13). Likewise, the end, that is, the completion or fullness of all evil, is the same idolatry; for nothing is lacking in any wickedness to him who worships the Devil as divine power; therefore, everything is reckoned to him as evil and sin.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Their whole life is established in errors; if they rejoice, either at festivals or in their games, they act madly, while they either commit murders or defile themselves obscenely with lust; while they prophesy, they deceive and lead their listeners astray; while they live unjustly, they are dead in soul; if they swear falsely, they are quickly led to hell; when they swear by idols, they pollute the name of God, who commands in the law, saying: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain (Ex. 20:7). And again: By the name, he says, of foreign gods you shall not swear, but by the name of the Lord your God (Ex. 23:13). But when they think they can mock God, they cast themselves into eternal death. Allegorically, however, heretics, worshipping the images of their errors, are themselves the cause of their own destruction, whose doctrine is false, life unjust, joy insane, and death abominable. For when they swear unjustly by an idol and do not hope in the true God, despising justice, they will receive the just punishment of their deeds. This is also consequently implied.
On the Trinity 1.1

The following dissertation concerning the Trinity, as the reader ought to be informed, has been written in order to guard against the sophistries of those who disdain to begin with faith, and are deceived by a crude and perverse love of reason. Now one class of such men endeavor to transfer to things incorporeal and spiritual the ideas they have formed, whether through experience of the bodily senses, or by natural human wit and diligent quickness, or by the aid of art, from things corporeal; so as to seek to measure and conceive of the former by the latter. Others, again, frame whatever sentiments they may have concerning God according to the nature or affections of the human mind; and through this error they govern their discourse, in disputing concerning God, by distorted and fallacious rules. While yet a third class strive indeed to transcend the whole creation, which doubtless is changeable, in order to raise their thought to the unchangeable substance, which is God; but being weighed down by the burden of mortality, whilst they both would seem to know what they do not, and cannot know what they would, preclude themselves from entering the very path of understanding, by an over-bold affirmation of their own presumptuous judgments; choosing rather not to correct their own opinion when it is perverse, than to change that which they have once defended. And, indeed, this is the common disease of all the three classes which I have mentioned,-viz., both of those who frame their thoughts of God according to things corporeal, and of those who do so according to the spiritual creature, such as is the soul; and of those who neither regard the body nor the spiritual creature, and yet think falsely about God; and are indeed so much the further from the truth, that nothing can be found answering to their conceptions, either in the body, or in the made or created spirit, or in the Creator Himself.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

By the just judgment of God, those who are condemned and repent too late recognize what, while living before, they refused to believe; therefore also the Psalmist bears witness, saying: The Lord will be known by executing judgments; the sinner is caught in the works of his own hands. The sinners shall be turned into Hades, all the nations that forget God (Ps. 9:16-18).

n: Mercy. The pagans have no real respect for their gods: they fear them not. (Calmet) --- But we know that Thou governest all, (Haydock) and will punish us, if we transgress. (Calmet)

Us. He wrote after the captivity, when the Jews abhorred idolatry, (Calmet) as they might also do at the beginning of Solomon's reign. (Haydock) --- Picture. It is not certain that the art was known in the days of Moses, or that he expressly forbade it. Pliny says it was discovered at Corinth, by making the outlines of a man's shadow on the wall. Afterwards one colour was used, till a variety was found to represent things more perfectly, (L. xxxv. 3, 4.) so as to deceive the senses, for which reason it is styled a fruitless labour. (Calmet)
Clay. In death, those who have trusted in creatures, shall be abandoned by all.
Worketh. God gives life, and also the rational soul, Genesis ii. 7.

Evil. This is the maxim of worldlings. (Calmet) --- Virtus post nummos. (Horace, i. ep. 1.) --- Our occupations are like those of children. They presently perish, or we must quit them. (St. Chrysostom, hom. xlvii. ad Pop.) --- We must strive to act our part well. Libertines deem this life a comedy, and represent religion as an imposition. (Calmet) --- They are like atheists, as they leave the true God, who seek gain by idols. (Worthington)

In their pride, they threaten more than they can perform, (Isaias xvi. 6.) or they take images to be gods, which infants only imagine are men, as Lactantius observes, quoting Lucilius,--- Ut pueri infantes credunt signa omnia ahena Vivere et esse homines. ----- (Haydock) --- Measure. They become insolent, and despise and persecute the servants of God. (Worthington)

Beasts. They are deformed, (Haydock) and seem to have been cursed by God, like the serpent, Genesis iii. 14. (Calmet) --- Fled from. Or "have banished" (Lorin.) God's praise, claiming it for themselves. (Menochius)

f: Against Marivadus the Arian, PL 62

On common truth. True Father, true Son, true Holy Spirit. Of the Father in Solomon: For our God, are kind and true: For to know you is complete righteousness (Wis. 15:1, 3). Of the Son in John: That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; this is the true God, and eternal life (1 Jn. 5:20). Of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel: When that Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, shall come, he will teach you all truth (Jn. 16:13).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Our God is gentle, for His love is indescribable. He is true, because He deceives no one and is deceived by no one. Patient and in mercy arranging all things; for because of His goodness He patiently endures us, waiting for us to turn for the better. Not wishing anyone to perish, but that all may be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. (1 Tim. 2:4) As He says through the prophet: I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 33:11). If we have sinned, we cannot escape His hand, because we are His creation. But if we cease to sin and persist in good works, we will receive a sure reward from Him, with whom the full number of all good deeds is kept. For He knows all, and no secret is hidden from Him. What His knowledge brings us is made clear by the following statement. For to know you is perfect justice, and to know your justice and virtue is the root of immortality. Whoever truly desires to know God strives to abstain from all sin, as the apostle John confirms, saying: Everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure (1 Jn. 3:3). And again: Everyone who abides in him does not sin; everyone who sins has not seen him nor known him (1 Jn. 3:6). But to know God is perfect justice, that is, the highest perfection of blessedness; and to know his justice and virtue is the root of immortality. But what is the justice and virtue of God except him of whom the Apostle says: I mean Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who has become for us from God wisdom and justice, sanctification and redemption. For to know God and his justice and virtue is the root of immortality (1 Cor. 1:30), that is, the perception of incorruption and the contemplation of truth in eternal life, as Truth itself says to the Father in the Gospel: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent; whom now we know in part by faith, but then we shall know in truth, just as we are known, for we shall see him as he is; for now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face (Jn. 17).
Tractate on the Gospel of John, 73.1

Do we not see how the Israelites got to their own hurt what their guilty lusting craved? For while it was raining manna on them from heaven, they desired to have flesh to eat. (Num. 11:32) They disdained what they had, and shamelessly sought what they had not: as if it were not better for them to have asked not to have their unbecoming desires gratified with the food that was wanting, but to have their own dislike removed, and be made themselves to receive aright the food that was provided. For when evil becomes our delight, and what is good the reverse, we ought to be entreating God rather to win us back to the love of the good, than to grant us the evil. Not that it is wrong to eat flesh, for the apostle, speaking of this very thing, says, Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused which is received with thanksgiving; (1 Tim. 4:4) but because, as he also says, It is evil for that man who eats with offense; (Rom. 14:20) and if so, with offense to man, how much more so if to God.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He speaks from the perspective of the faithful, who, fortified by the grace of God, in no way wish to involve themselves in the wickedness of the pagans, nor do they deem it worthy to imitate the errors they have in idolatry and various crimes, because such labor is without the fruit of righteousness; indeed, it deserves eternal death.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Not only therefore are those who make idols guilty, but also those who love and worship them, placing their hope in them, are guilty and transgressors, because not only those who do evil, but also those who consent to those who do evil are worthy of death. The kind of people who place their hope in their idols is shown by the Psalmist, saying: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but do not speak, they have eyes but do not see. They have ears but do not hear, they have noses but do not smell. They have hands but do not feel, they have feet but do not walk, they do not make a sound in their throats; for there is no breath in their mouths. May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them (Ps. 115:4-8). For a mortal fashions a dead thing with wicked hands and the fool worships the most foolish thing. In an allegorical sense, the inventors and builders of perverse doctrines are heresiarchs; their lovers and worshipers are their followers and disciples, all of whom are guilty and liable to destruction: For all will tremble and stand, and together be confounded (Isa. 44:11). For the Lord will destroy the man who has done this, both the master and his disciple (Mal. 2:12). Woe to their souls, for evil has been repaid to them (Isa. 3:11).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Previously, he had spoken about those who had made idols from wood or stones or certain metals; now he also speaks about those who, following the same vanity in the craft of the potter, are shown to be equally guilty through a similar error. For the pagans themselves have fallen into such foolishness that not only did they make idols from gold or silver, or even from precious stones, but they also fashioned images in the same way from cheap clay, calling a god that which was formed from the clay of the earth by the work of a potter. Therefore, it was justly repaid to them that, since they were made from the earth and did not wish to follow the better part of themselves, that is, the rational soul which is created in the image of God, to worship the living God, by imitating the baser part of themselves, that is, the earthly body, they worshipped a clay god. Therefore, afterwards, without the fruit of good works, they themselves, senseless and useless, were rendered to the insensible earth from which they were taken. Mystically, all heretics and schismatics who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness and worship a lie instead of the truth in the images of their doctrines, even if they sometimes possess attractive speech or seem to have reasonable virtues, will nevertheless be proven to be altogether fragile, as if made of clay, because they invent useless things. Therefore, their heart is ashes, that is, their thought is foul, and their life is more sleazy than any mud, because they are ignorant of Him who formed them and gave them an intelligent mind. Instead, they vanish in their own thoughts, despising the understanding of the holy Fathers, which those Fathers had in the divine Scriptures through the gift of the Holy Spirit. They shamelessly establish new errors, as if vain amusements, for human favor and earthly gain, wandering themselves and leading into error whomever they can, so that they may be inexcusable on the day of judgment, when the Judge of all shall come to judge the secrets of hearts and render to each according to his works.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Heretics have no excuse, for they sin knowingly, when they refuse to follow the holy and catholic teachers in right faith and sound doctrine, but according to their own perverse inventions, they choose rather an earthly and fragile understanding than to strive for a spiritual and heavenly one in their dogmas. For all fools are excessively proud in their souls.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Indeed, the proud enemies of the people of God and all enemies of justice, although they may seem to rule on earth for a time, yet because they are foolish, they consider the senseless idols of the nations to be gods, which have neither sight, nor hearing, nor touch, nor any sense of life; they are most unhappy, awaiting the destruction of their souls in Gehenna, where there will be perpetual punishment of torment; for their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched, because they did not give honor to the living and true God, and served carved images which they themselves wickedly made (Mark 9:44-48).
Sermon 23B

You say God lies, but you are convicted by the very one you made. Nor because you are convicted by it, will it be better than you; even if you lie, it does not lie, you call it god, it calls itself wood, it will not be better than you. Not for you to have a reason to want to worship something better. You feel, it does not feel; you hear and it does not hear; you see and it does not see; you walk and it does not walk; you live and I cannot say: It is dead, because it never lived. You are better than the one you made; worship the one better than you, who made you. It is an insult to you to be like the one you made. What sort of thing should you worship? You get angry at someone cursing you if they say: "Be like this," and yet you worship what you detest being, and by worshiping you become somewhat similar, not that you become wood and cease to be human, but you make your inner man somewhat like the thing you made outwardly.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For man is better than idols according to the reason of his creation, because he himself lives and understands, but they never do. Yet, because he has followed the vanity of error more than the knowledge of truth, it is fulfilled in him what is said by the Psalmist: Man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts, and became like them (Psalm 49:20).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Miserable paganism not only worshipped the human form shaped in insensible things as a deity, but also perversely adored the forms of other animals, nor did it have a just discernment in any matter. For according to the consideration of truth, living things are set before the dead, and sensible things before insensible, and rational animals before other animals; but it was fitting that those who ignored their Creator also did not know how to make proper distinctions among His creatures; for whoever neglects to have the praise and blessing of God within himself will prove himself to err in the observation and discernment of animals.

n: Things. Septuagint, "therefore by similar things they," &c. (Haydock) --- The Egyptians were punished for their idolatry by beasts, though they worshipped them, (Haydock) being infested with insects, frogs, locusts, &c., (chap. xii. 23., and Exodus viii., and x.; Calmet) and seeing their first-born perish for their cruelty. (Worthington)

Meat. The second time, God gave them in his anger: but still he dealt favourably with his people, (Exodus xvi. 13., and Numbers xi. 7.; Calmet) punishing them as a father, for their amendment. (Worthington)

They indeed desiring food, &c. He means the Egyptians; who were restrained even from that food which was necessary, by the frogs and the flies that were sent amongst them, and spoiled all their meats. (Challoner) --- Exodus viii. 3. (Calmet) --- These. The Israelites. (Challoner) --- New meat. Quails. (Menochius)

Sign of salvation. The brazen serpent, an emblem of Christ our Saviour; (Challoner) and of the obedience which they should shew to God's commands. (Calmet) --- The sign could have no inherent value; but, as a token of God's favour, was the means of curing the people. (Worthington)
Plaster, malagma. The remedy ordained by God was not naturally efficacious. (Calmet) --- "Every wound of the soul has its medicine in the Scriptures." (St. Augustine, Psalm xxxvi.)

The fire had more force. Viz., When the fire and hail mingled together laid waste the land of Egypt, Exodus ix. (Challoner) --- This destroyed the useful cattle, but not such as infested the Egyptians. (Worthington) --- The water seemed to nourish the flames, 3 Kings xviii. 39.

Mitigated. The Egyptians could not banish the insects with fire and smoke, (Jansenius) or the storm sent by God, did not exterminate the sciniphs, which had caused the magicians to acknowledge a miracle, Exodus viii. 18. The frogs and flies were already gone, Ibid.[Exodus viii.?] 11., and 31. (Calmet)

Angels. See Exodus xvi. (Worthington) --- If angels stood in need of food, they could have nothing more delicious. So water is styled honey, to denote its excellence, Psalm lxxvii. 25., Leviticus xx. 24., and Joel iii. 18. --- Taste. These expressions are figurative. (Calmet)

Sustenance. Literally, "substance," which some explain (Calmet) of God himself preparing this delicious food. (Naz. or. xlix.) --- Liked. So that if a person wished to eat an egg, &c., the manna became one, without altering its appearance, which is the case in the blessed Eucharist. (Valentia, 4 disp. 6., &c.) --- But this opinion supposes a continued miracle, which seems not necessary, and it is generally believed that the taste alone was changed, which St. Augustine and others restrain to God's faithful servants, otherwise the Hebrews could not have been disgusted with manna, Numbers xi. 6., and xxi. 5. To these it was therefore simply manna. But the others found in it whatever they could desire. (St. Gregory, Mor. vi. 9.) --- Yet according to others, (Haydock) both enjoyed the same privilege. (Menochius) --- We cannot account for men's fancies.
Word. Deuteronomy viii. 3., and Matthew iv. 4. Fruits, of themselves, could not support man. (Calmet)
Light. Those who desire to receive any favour must seek it with diligence, as the manna was to be gathered before sun-rise. (Clarius.) (Calmet)

Water. The ungrateful and negligent shall find their hopes frustrated, (Calmet) as well as the wicked, who expect salvation (Worthington) without a change of manners. (Haydock) --- Ingratitude stops the fountain of grace. (Menochius)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

If you refer this to the Egyptians, who, being idolaters and given to various errors, also unjustly persecuted the people of God, in those ten plagues with which the Lord punished them because they were unwilling to let His people go, it can be understood that they experienced the viciousness of beasts; for there, too, flies of various kinds and locusts are described as having devastated them, likewise frogs and reptiles and other creatures of the earth, of which it is written in the psalm: He sent among them swarms of flies, which devoured them; frogs, which destroyed them; and He gave their fruits to the caterpillar, and their labors to the locust (Ps. 78:45-47). In another sense, heretics and schismatics and all the wicked are also torn, scattered, and destroyed by spiritual beasts, that is, by evil spirits, to whose will they consented and, by the just judgment of God, were subjected to their power, so that they might torment and scatter them.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It is read in the Book of Numbers that when the Israelite people desired to eat meat in the desert, the Lord provided them with a multitude of quails, which they ate until they were satisfied to the point of nausea; nevertheless, the punishment for their desire was not far from them, for the wrath of the Lord, stirred up against the people, struck them with a very great plague, and the place was called the grave of desire (Num. 11). Therefore, wisdom now remembers this, alternating its discussion about the destruction of the Egyptians and the correction of the Israelites, because those who resisted God and exercised tyranny over His people perished suddenly without excuse. However, these were corrected for a time and punished three times in a manner suitable for discipline, yet they were not entirely deprived of divine comfort.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It is read in the aforementioned book of Numbers that the murmuring children of Israel, in the thirty-fifth encampment, because of the weariness of the journey and labor, and the lack of food, aroused the anger of the Lord against themselves. Therefore, the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and after many had been wounded and killed by them, they came to Moses and said: We have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord and against you; pray that He may take the serpents away from us. Moses prayed for the people, and the Lord spoke to him: Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; whoever is bitten and looks at it shall live. So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign, and when those who had been bitten looked at it, they were healed (Num. 21:6-9). But it must be carefully considered what is said: For he who was healed was not healed by what he saw, but by You, the Savior of all. For it was not the bronze serpent, which was set up as a sign in a figurative way, that saved them, but the ritual of the mystery, that is, the death of Christ, who was prefigured in that serpent; He Himself saved the human race: for all these things happened to them as a figure. Moreover, they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. But what does it mean that wounds in men caused by the bite of wild serpents were healed by the raising up and looking at the bronze serpent, unless it is that now, in the type of the Savior, who on the wood of the cross triumphed over the wild and ancient serpent, the venom of the Devil is overcome? So that whoever truly and clearly beholds the image of the Son of God and His passion is preserved. For this is also signified by the words of the Lord Himself, saying: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may not perish, but may have eternal life (Jn. 3:14-15). Therefore, rightly was it a bronze serpent that was suspended on the wood; for bronze is usually more durable than other metals, and openly the bronze serpent was suspended on the wood, so that the Lord might be signified both as dead in the serpent and as eternal in the bronze; namely, that He might be shown as dead through His humanity, and yet, as it were, bronze, because of His divinity.
HOMILIES ON JOSHUA 4.2

There is a priestly and Levitical order which is to show the way to the people of God who have gone out from Egypt. For it is they who teach the people to go out from Egypt, that is, from the errors of the world, and to pass through the vast wilderness, that is, to traverse the various kinds of temptations and not to be harmed by the serpents, which are the bites of demons, and to avoid the poisons of evil suggestions. And "if" perhaps "someone has been struck" in the wilderness "by a serpent," that they may show him the "bronze serpent" hung upon the cross, "which whoever shall look upon," that is, whoever believes in him whose figure that serpent displayed, shall through this flee from the diabolical poisons.
Sermon 20.2

But the mention of locusts in the eighth place, I think, through this kind of plague or detractor, or always by its own discord, is intended to signify the inconsistency of the human race. For the locust, although it has no king, as Scripture says, leads its army in order with one line (Prov. 30:27); but men, although made rational by God, have neither been able to govern themselves in an orderly manner, nor have they patiently endured the moderation of God the King.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

A distinction must be noted, because just as punishment sometimes tests and admonishes the elect, so that they may avoid sins and persist in works of righteousness, and diligently observe the faith of God and the keeping of His commandments, so also correction applied to the depraved casts them down and destroys them, since no correction or worthy change is found in them; therefore, by the will of God, small animals killed the idolaters, and conversely, the Israelites, worshippers of the true God, could not be exterminated by the venom of serpents, because the Lord knows how to rescue the virtuous from temptation, but to keep the wicked for torment on the day of judgment.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Note that he says those harmed by serpents were not healed by bandages and the work of doctors, but by the Word of the Lord, that is, the Son through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made: whose power rules everywhere, and does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths; he himself heals bodies, he himself saves both bodies and souls from spiritual beasts, that is, evil spirits, nor is there anyone who can resist his will (Esther 13:11).
No One Can Harm the Man Who Does Not Harm Himself 4

Man, through malice and wickedness, that is, by his own will and the effect of wrongful action, kills the soul. Therefore someone has said: no one can be harmed except by himself, because he is either the originator of his own crime or consents to the crimes of others. For if a man guards his mind and does not consent to evil persuasion, he is free from all guilt.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

By the hatred of man the soul is slain, that is, by the wickedness of one's own will and the effect of evil deeds. Therefore someone has said: No one can be harmed except by himself, because he is either the inventor of his own crime, or the supporter and encourager of another's wickedness. For if a man guards his mind and does not consent to evil persuasion, he is free from all guilt.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

When Moses compelled Pharaoh by the word of the Lord to allow the children of Israel to depart from Egypt so that they might sacrifice to the Lord in the desert, Pharaoh, hardened in his profane speech, replied: I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go (Ex. 5). Therefore, he was struck with various plagues together with his people, among which he was struck by hail and fire at the same time, as it is read in Exodus: for hail and fire were mingled and carried together, and struck everything that was in the fields, from man to beast, and the hail struck every herb of the field, and broke every tree of the region (Ex. 9:24-25). Nor is it surprising that two contrary elements, that is, fire and hail, struck together, since all things obey the will of their Creator, and there is no opposition where the divine majesty commands. For at one time the fire was gentle so that the animals sent by the wicked would not be burned, but so that those who saw would know that they suffered persecution by the judgment of God. And at another time, fire burned above the power of water everywhere to destroy the wicked nation of the land. Therefore, just as it is read in the book of Genesis that the Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah to destroy the wicked (Gen. 19), and in Exodus it is told that a mixture of hail and fire struck the wicked (Ex. 9), so in the book of Numbers it is mentioned that fiery serpents destroyed the rebellious and murmurers, so that the stubborn might recognize that every creature is prepared for the vengeance of the wicked, when they do not fear to rebel against the commands of their Creator (Num. 21).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Here wisdom commemorates for the people of Israel in the desert the manna, the sweetest and healthiest food given from heaven, so that they might render greater thanks to their Redeemer, who not only mercifully freed them from their enemies when they were oppressed, but also generously fed them with heavenly provisions when they were in need (Ex. 16). If anyone thinks it necessary to inquire what is meant by saying that snow and ice withstand the force of fire and do not melt, let him understand that it was not made known there, that two contrary elements, namely fire and frozen water, struck the wicked in harmony, or that some quality of the heavenly food given as food to the people of God was expressed there, which endured the force of fire where it was necessary, and yet, when it was necessary, melted in the heat of the sun. It is also read in Exodus that in the wilderness appeared something white, small, and cut like hair, resembling frost upon the ground, the taste of which was like flour mixed with honey, nor did it suffer any loss from the force of fire. Therefore it is written in the book of Numbers: Now the manna was like coriander seed, the color of bdellium; and the people went about gathering it, grinding it in mills or pounding it in mortars, cooking it in pots and making cakes of it, the taste of which was like bread made with oil. But when the sun rose, it melted (Num. 11:7-15). Mystically, just as in the scourge of hail and fire there is a harsh rebuke, so divine Scripture is understood to torment sinners, so also in the heavenly food there is a heavenly comfort, which daily refreshes the righteous and those devoted to God. Otherwise, manna signifies that bread which in the Gospel says: I am the bread of life who came down from heaven, and I give life to the world. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst. And again: The bread, he says, which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world. And again: Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him (Jn. 6:35-40). Whoever therefore truly attains to the participation of this bread will undoubtedly possess eternal life without end. Therefore, the reprobate are tormented by spiritual hunger, and the elect are healthily fed by the heavenly bread: the former are daily prepared by various labors for future punishment; the latter, however, are daily nourished by divine help for eternal life. Which the Prophet also testifies, saying: Many are the sorrows of the wicked; but mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord (Ps. 32:10).
Morals on Job, PL 75-76, 2.2.22

As a certain wise man says about the sweetness of manna: You provided them with ready bread from heaven without labor, containing every delight and all the sweetness of taste (Wis. 16:20). For manna indeed contained every delight and all sweetness of taste, because, in the mouths of the spiritual, it gave flavor according to the will of those who ate, since the divine word is both suitable for all and not inconsistent with itself, adapting to the capacity of the hearers; and when each chosen person profitably understands it according to his own measure, he transforms the manna received into a flavor of his own choosing.
Against Marivadus the Arian, PL 62

Where they say that the Son was not born from the substance of the Father. But if they should say: the Son was not born from the paternal substance, but generated from another substance. Response. We also, who confess the Father and the Son to be of one substance, have taught by divine authority that the Son is from the substance of God the Father, as the prophet Jeremiah says: "Take up mourning over the minds, and lamentation over the paths of the desert, because they have failed, since they are not men; because they were unwilling to hear the voice of my substance, from the birds of the sky even to the beasts they have fallen away in mind" (Jer. 9:10). Likewise there: "Who has stood in the substance of the Lord, and will see the word of God? Who has given ear and heard" (Jer. 23:18)? And there: "If they had stood in my substance, and if they had heard my words, and if they had taught my people, I would have turned them away from their most evil pursuits" (Jer. 23:22). And the Apostle: "Who, being the radiance of glory and the form of his substance" (Heb. 1:3). Likewise he himself: "For we have become partakers of God; let us hold fast the beginning of his substance" (Heb. 3:14). And in Solomon: "My substance is my sweetness" (Wis. 16:21). From this, then, recognize that he who is called the substance of God the Father is not believed to be foreign to that same substance.
History of the Persecution of the African Province, PL 58, 3.23.3

Therefore, the substance of the Father is designated as the Son by the prophetic oracles long ago, as Solomon says: For you showed your substance and sweetness, which you have for your sons (Wis. 16:21), which appeared to have flowed down to the people of Israel from heaven in the form and image of heavenly bread. The Lord Himself explained this in the Gospel, saying: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you bread from heaven (Jn. 6:32); clearly designating Himself as the bread when He says: I am the living bread which came down from heaven (Ibid. 41). Of whom also the prophet David says: Man ate the bread of angels (Ps. 77:25). For in order to show even more clearly the unity of substance and equality of divinity between the Father and the Son, He Himself says in the Gospel: I am in the Father, and the Father is in me. And: I and the Father are one (Jn. 10:38, 30). This refers not only to the unity of will, but to one and the same substance.
On the Trinity 2.11

For the Spirit did not beatify the dove, or the wind, or the fire, and join them for ever to Himself and to His person in unity and "fashion." Nor, again, is the nature of the Holy Spirit mutable and changeable; so that these things were not made of the creature, but He himself was turned and changed first into one and then into another, as water is changed into ice. But these things appeared at the seasons at which they ought to have appeared, the creature serving the Creator, and being changed and converted at the command of Him who remains immutably in Himself, in order to signify and manifest Him in such way as it was fit He should be signified and manifested to mortal men. Accordingly, although that dove is called the Spirit; and in speaking of that fire, "There appeared unto them," he says, "cloven tongues, like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them; and they began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance;" in order to show that the Spirit was manifested by that fire, as by the dove; yet we cannot call the Holy Spirit both God and a dove, or both God and fire, in the same way as we call the Son both God and man.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

By this sentence all the wicked and sinners are confused, because while the rest of creation serves its Creator, they alone are found to resist His will and commands. But since no one can resist His will, they are deservedly scourged and corrected by the harmony of all creatures, and if they do not repent nor improve themselves, they will be handed over to be tormented with perpetual punishments. But for the good alone true goods are prepared, while for the wicked unending torments are appointed.
ON THE TRINITY 3:1.6

Our present inquiry then is, whether the angels were then the agents both in showing those bodily appearances to the eyes of men and in sounding those words in their ears, when the sensible creature itself, serving the Creator at His beck, was turned for the time into whatever was needful; as it is written in the book of Wisdom, "For the creature serveth Thee, who art the Maker, increaseth his strength against the unrighteous for their punishment, and abateth his strength for the benefit of such as put their trust in Thee. Therefore, even then was it altered into all fashions, and was obedient to Thy grace, that nourisheth all things according to the desire of them that longed for Thee." For the power of the will of God reaches through the spiritual creature even to visible and sensible effects of the corporeal creature. For where does not the wisdom of the omnipotent God work that which He wills, which "reacheth from one end to another mightily, and sweetly doth order all things"?
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, the people of God in the desert were comforted by various support and cherished by divine mercy. Manna rained down for them from heaven, most abundant water was given to them from the rock, they were fed with the flesh of birds, their garments were not worn out, nor were their shoes consumed; during the day the sun did not burn them, because He led them in a cloud by day, and all night in the illumination of fire, so that they might become more devoted to their Creator, who helped them freely by providing for every necessity. For this reason He cared for them temporarily, so that they might love and understand Him perpetually, according to the mention of this place, since it is not the fruits of birth that feed men, but the word of God preserves those who believe in Him. Moses also proves this in Deuteronomy, saying: He afflicted you with want, and gave you the food of manna, which you and your fathers did not know, to show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Your garment with which you were clothed did not fail through age, and your foot was not worn out. Behold, it is the fortieth year, so that you may reflect in your heart, because just as a man instructs his son, so the Lord your God has instructed you, that you may keep the commandments of your God, and walk in His ways, and fear Him; for the Lord your God will bring you into a good land (Deut. 8:3–7). But because they were always ungrateful and clung to figures, they did not wish to receive the truth itself coming to them; therefore, all things were transferred to the fruits of the Holy Church; for all things happened to them in figure. Moreover, they were written for our correction, as Paul also clearly proved, writing to the Corinthians, saying: For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:1-4). For Christ is the foundation of the whole law and the truth of the figures; whoever believes in Him has fulfilled the whole law; but whoever does not believe, as a transgressor of the law, will perish eternally.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

We have already said above that the manna, which endured the odor of fire, would melt at the heat of the sun; but now, since he repeats the same mystery, we believe it is enough to speak of its meaning. For that figurative food fed our fathers in a historical sense, but it melted at the rising of the true sun, that is, at the birth of Christ it was dissolved for spiritual use and was transformed into a heavenly ritual, so that we may anticipate the sun in blessings, that is, proclaim the divinity of Christ with eternal praises, saying with the evangelist John: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God: all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, etc. (Jn. 1:1-3). But at the rising of the light, that is, at the coming of the Savior, let us say: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, the glory as of the only begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. But let us see what follows concerning that carnal people.
ON PRAYER 31:1

It seems to me that, to complete the argument of the prayer, it would not be out of place after this to discuss briefly the disposition and the attitude that one who prays must have, as well as the place where one should pray and the direction he should face (if circumstances permit) and the choice of the appropriate time for praying, and topics of this kind. Disposition refers to the soul, attitude to the body. Thus Paul says … one must pray "without anger or dissension." The attitude consists in "raising pure hands," expressions that seem to me to be derived from the psalms, which say, "May the raising of my hands be like the evening sacrifice." Regarding the place, "I want therefore that people pray in every place." Regarding the orientation, the Wisdom of Solomon says, "To make it known that one must rise before the sun to give you thanks and worship you before the dawning of the light."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 25:4-5

No one hath so labored that we should be approved, and great, and in all things right-minded, as the God who made us. Wherefore both against our will He befriends us often, and without our knowledge oftener than not. And if thou marvel at what I have said, I point to this as having occurred not to any ordinary person, but to the blessed Paul. For even that blessed man, when in much danger and affliction, often besought God that the temptations might depart from him: nevertheless God regarded not his request, but his profit, and to signify this He said, "My grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness." So that before He hath told him the reason, He benefits him against his will, and without his knowing it.

Now what great thing doth He ask, in requiring us to be thankful in return for such tender care? Let us then obey, and everywhere keep up this. Since neither were the Jews by anything ruined so much, as by being unthankful; those many stripes, one after another, were brought upon them by nothing else than this; or rather even before those stripes this had ruined and corrupted their soul. "For the hope of the unthankful," saith one, "is like the winter's hoar frost;" it benumbs and deadens the soul, as that doth our bodies.

And this springs from pride, and from thinking one's self worthy of something. But the contrite will acknowledge grounds of thanksgiving to God, not for good things only, but also for what seem to be adverse; and how much soever he may suffer, will count none of his sufferings undeserved. Let us then also, the more we advance in virtue, so much the more make ourselves contrite; for indeed this, more than anything else is virtue.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the hopes of the people, that is, the Jews' hope which they now have for the coming of their king, namely the Antichrist, melts away like winter ice, that is, it withers cold in unbelief without the fruit of righteousness, and will perish like surplus water, when all the tradition of their doctrine is deemed of no use; for our Savior, speaking to the apostles, says to us: Let them alone, they are blind leaders of the blind. Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt. 15:13-14).

n: Souls. The Egyptians, who were punished with horrible darkness, as they had followed an unjust, dark, and cruel policy against the Hebrews.

Providence, and day-light, like incorrigible slaves, in prison. (Calmet) --- The Egyptians were three days in darkness, (Exodus x. 22.) and the Gentiles continued without faith in God, till after Christ's resurrection. (Worthington) --- Only few served him, before that glorious event.

Sins. This interior darkness was punished with the exterior one. (Calmet) --- Forgetfulness. Of each other, being concerned only for themselves, (Haydock) or they seemed to be forgotten by Providence, or buried in Lethean, most dismal obscurity. The interpreter thus mentions Cocytus, without sanctioning poetical fables, Job xxi. 33. (Menochius) --- Exceeding. Greek, "spectres." (Calmet)
Fire. Like lightning, which would not allow them leisure to distinguish objects. (Calmet)
Rebuked. Or chastised. (Haydock) --- The magicians could not imitate this miracle, nor secure themselves from its horrors. (Calmet)

Fear. the Egyptians kept serpents in their houses, and fed them. But now, neglecting to shew this attention, they were affrighted with their hissing. --- Air. Or could live. They seemed to wish for death, (Calmet) like the damned, but it fled from them. (Haydock)
Things. The wicked are most cowardly. (Calmet) --- "Crimes may be safe; they cannot be secure." (Seneca, ep. xcvii.)
Thought. And giving way to despair, when it is extreme.
Expectation. Or fear. Such an one is filled with a mortal anxiety.
Them. From the sight of spectres, and remorse of conscience.
Irons. Darkness forced them to stay where they were. (Calmet)
Birds. Nothing can afford comfort to the affrighted. (Menochius)

f: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6:53-54

In the Apocalypse we see "a Lamb, as though sacrificed." This is the Lamb that, for certain ineffable reasons, became the sacrifice of expiation for the entire world, having accepted even to be sacrificed, according to the measure of the Father's love for humanity. By his blood he bought us back from him who had bought us, in that we were corrupted by sins. Leading this lamb to the sacrifice was the God who was in the man, the great high priest, as he himself attests, saying, "No one takes my life from me, but I myself give it. I have the power to give it and the power to take it up again." All of the other sacrifices are related to this sacrifice by affinity, the sacrifices prescribed by the Law being a symbol of it. And in my opinion, the shedding of blood on the part of the noble martyrs are sacrifices similar to this one; not without reason does John the disciple contemplate them as surrounding the heavenly altar. "Who is wise enough to understand these things, intelligent enough to know them?" To grasp somewhat more contemplatively the reason for these sacrifices, which purify those for whom they are offered, we must understand the significance of the sacrifice of the daughter of Jephthah. Jephthah had defeated the Ammonites because of a vow, to which she who was to be sacrificed adhered, responding to her father's words, "I have given my word to the Lord against you," by saying, "Even if it is against me that you have given your word to the Lord, fulfill your vow." In considering such events one could be led to attribute an element of great cruelty to God, to whom such sacrifices are offered for the salvation of human beings. One needs a more open and farsighted mind to reconcile this in light of the designs of providence, so as to be able to justify these things as both ineffable and beyond human nature, saying, "The judgments of God are great and difficult to tell. For this reason, ignorant souls fell into error." Moreover, it is also attested among the pagans that in times of pestilence, many were given over to sacrifice for the common salvation. The faithful Roman Clement also admits that this occurred, basing himself on history; Paul testifies of him saying, "Together with Clement and my other coworkers, whose names are in the book of life." Someone wanting to insult mysteries that escape the comprehension of the many finds the precepts regarding martyrs similarly absurd. God, however, considers that it would be better for us to confess his divinity at the price of the most atrocious sufferings than to free ourselves for a brief time from apparent evils, declaring our acquiescence to the will of the enemies of truth.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Great are the judgments of the almighty God, and inexpressible are the words by which, with wondrous command, He governs all creation. For this reason, the senseless souls of unbelievers have gone astray, because they were unwilling to believe and understand their Creator, who made all things by His word, nor did they render to Him the due honor in the worship of devotion. Nor is it contrary to this statement, that the words of God are indescribable, what the Psalmist says: I have declared with my lips all the judgments of your mouth (Ps. 119:13), because those things which He wished to be declared by the mouth, that is, to be made revealed, human frailty can understand and recount; but those things which He Himself has decreed to remain hidden, no one at all has been able to investigate.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It commemorates the fact that in Egypt the enemies of the people of God suffered in the darkness of gloom, which Scripture reports as so dense that it could be felt; in which, having suffered excessive horror, they were justly punished for their sins and for the dark oblivion. Mystically, all persecutors of the Church of Christ, namely Jews, pagans, heretics, and also false Christians, suffer the enormous darkness of their crimes and errors, nor can they be safe and secure anywhere, for the rulers of these darknesses lead them according to their own will, and finally plunge them into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, to be punished perpetually with them. That all those who act wickedly are in darkness is shown by Truth itself in the Gospel, saying: “Everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light lest his works be reproved; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifest, because they are done in God” (Jn. 3:20-21). And again: “He who follows me,” he says, “will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (Jn. 8:12). Therefore John also says: “He who hates his brother is still in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 Jn. 2:11). Of which Peter also says to believers: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light, who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; and who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1 Peter 2:9-10). Therefore Paul also says to them: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. 5:8).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Horror always accompanies darkness, and the less one can see or discern the things around oneself, the greater fear one has, suspecting adversity on all sides and dreading harm. Therefore, it also happened to the Egyptians, when they endured the greatest darkness for three days, which neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even the stars could illuminate: wherever they hid, they trembled with excessive terror. But when it is said that sad figures appeared to them, causing fear, it could have happened that, by the scheming of evil spirits, certain phantasms appeared to them, which struck them with excessive horror to increase their punishments. Similarly, even now, the persecutors of the Christian faith and the enemies of truth are surrounded everywhere by the darkness of their sins, because they are ignorant of the sun of righteousness, nor do holy teachers illuminate them in any way with the brightness of their doctrines. These also are disturbed by a descending sound, that is, the heavenly preaching foretelling the punishments to come for them, and sad figures, that is, demons who are to torture them, terrify them beforehand; yet this does not generate fruitful repentance in them, but rather, having become worse, they are prepared without ceasing for eternal destruction: for since they despair of themselves, nor do they wish to correct themselves so as to abandon their error and do works of righteousness, they are storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For from that fire, which was punishing the wicked, they were terrified with fear, dreading punishments on all sides, because the more severe the pains of punishment one feels, the greater the horrors he fears may come upon him.
Augustine of Hippo, On Various Questions 79.3-4 PL 40

But when he says that false prophets will perform many signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect (Matt. 24:24), he certainly warns us to understand that even wicked men can perform certain miracles, which the saints cannot do; yet they are not therefore to be considered as having a higher place with God. For the Egyptian magicians were not more acceptable to God than the people of Israel, because that people could not do what the magicians did; although Moses, by the power of God, could do greater things (Ex. 7–12). But these things are not granted to all the saints, lest the weak be deceived by the most pernicious error, thinking that greater gifts are found in such deeds than in works of righteousness, by which eternal life is obtained. Therefore the Lord forbids the disciples to rejoice in this, when he says: Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Therefore, when magicians perform such things as saints sometimes do, these things indeed appear visibly, but are done with a different purpose and by a different right. For the magicians do them seeking their own glory, while the saints do them seeking the glory of God; and the magicians do them through certain powers granted in their own order, as if by private dealings or sorcery; but the saints do them by public administration, by the command of Him to whom all creation is subject.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

How the magi in Egypt resisted Moses by performing false wonders through magical incantations to deceive the people, the book of Exodus recalls; but at last, when they saw themselves overcome by the power of the signs which were divinely performed through Moses and Aaron, they were compelled to confess that it was the finger of God who accomplished these great deeds (Ex. 4:30). And those who just before boasted themselves to be healers of all diseases, at the coming of the serpents and other animals which afflicted them, were struck with fear and suffered in the same way as the others; and so also now, in the times of grace, all who mock the Christian religion, who boast in their own arts, that is, the diviners and soothsayers of the pagans, as well as those who have departed from the unity of the Church through apostasy, such as heretics and schismatics, although they pretend to be victorious, are nevertheless truly overcome by the power of Christ, and in the end will suffer the most cruel enemy, the ancient serpent, with his followers.
Gregory the Great, Morals on Job, PL 75-76. 2.27.25

Therefore, it is well said by a certain wise man: Since wickedness is fearful, it bears witness to its own condemnation (Wis. 17:10). For while fear, striking the conscience because of the deed, reproves, it gives itself damning testimony for the case it commits. On the contrary, it is said by John: If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God (1 Jn. 3:21). Therefore, let the wicked flee from human eyes, but they certainly cannot flee from themselves. For since they know the evil they do, they have conscience as a witness, and their own reason as a judge. Therefore, in the sin they commit, they first encounter the judgment of their own reason against themselves. And this is perhaps what is said by the Psalmist: Deep calls to deep at the sound of your waterfalls (Ps. 42:8). For, by a wondrous order of hidden arrangement, the evil that is done is not permitted to be unknown, and the sinner already condemns himself in his conscience by his own judgment, and after his own condemnation hastens to the sentence of the eternal Judge. Therefore, for deep to call to deep is to pass from judgment to judgment.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For in this, he says that those wicked men denied seeing the air, whose presence no living and breathing animal can ever avoid; he expresses the excess of fear, which, because of the oppression of impending punishments, they suffer as their own evil rebukes their conscience. Moreover, since wickedness is always fearful, its own terror gives rise to punishments when it is condemned.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the conscience is always troubled, and if it does not have the serenity of tranquility within itself, it arrogantly elevates itself, but this presumption is restrained by fear itself. Therefore it is said that his fear is a help, that is, a remedy. It also reveals the weakness of the proud mind, which, by imagining vain hopes of help, was driving itself mad, when it hoped it could achieve what it could in no way accomplish; and therefore, as its inner health was less than the things it suffered outwardly, it thought its power was greater. This often happens also among the persecutors of the faithful; for, because of the blindness of their hearts, they consider themselves powerful when they torture the bodies of the saints with various torments, but when, overcome by their patience, they see that they cannot achieve what they wanted, they are crushed by the anguish of their own mind, and at last they recognize that they are not what they previously thought themselves to be, and they realize that he is stronger who granted his soldiers patience, the endurance to suffer punishments, and the strength to overcome their enemies.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

He says this when, in Egypt, the enemies of the people of God were surrounded by the horror of darkness, so that neither those awake nor those asleep had any rest. For either those sleeping were disturbed by terrifying visions, or those awake were tormented by excessive fear; nor was there any opportunity given to them to withdraw freely anywhere, but without a shackle or iron chain, they were confined in the prison of darkness. Therefore it is written: For three days, no one saw his brother, nor did anyone move from the place where he was (Ex. 10:23).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109
For on every side the wretched were constrained by punishment, for whatever they perceived with their ears from sound, or sensed by any feeling, they feared that all was aimed at their destruction.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For only the wicked were in darkness; but the worshippers of God abounded in the most abundant light. Therefore, it is written: But wherever the children of Israel dwelt, there was light (Ex. 10:23). But it must also be considered what is said: Only for them there was a heavy night, an image of the darkness that was to come upon them, for they themselves were a heavier darkness to themselves. In this it is clearly shown that spiritual darkness, which the mind suffers, is heavier than bodily darkness, which the eye endures; for from these darknesses, that is, of unbelief and error and wickedness, a man is led to the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; which darkness of the Egyptians prefigured, for just as there bodies were held useless for every good work, so here both bodies and souls are shut up in eternal prison, unfit for every good work, because neither reason, nor place, nor time for working is found among the dead.

n: Their. The Hebrews' (Menochius) or rather the Egyptians' voice. The land of Gossen was preserved from these horrors, (Calmet) though such Egyptians as might be found there, were exposed to them; and their dismal lamentations made the people of God appreciate their own happiness. They are styled saints, (Haydock) as the Church is holy, and has always some saints in her society. Out of it there is no sanctity. (Worthington)

Therefore. "Instead of those things, " (Greek) darkness and complaints, (Haydock) God led away his people in triumph. (Habacuc iii. 3.) --- A harmless sun. A light that should not hurt or molest them; but that should be an agreeable guest to them; (Challoner) or the desert should receive them, where they should be provided with food. (Menochius)

Was. Literally, "began." (Haydock) --- In Egypt, the Hebrews themselves were unacquainted with the law, which was given at their arrival at Sinai, and by means of the Greek version, and the propagation of the gospel, it was more divulged. (Calmet) --- The unwritten law was, however, better preserved in that nation, than in any other: and the Jews were selected, in order that they might communicate the treasure to all. (Haydock)
One child. Viz., Moses. (Challoner) --- He was preserved to be the leader of the Hebrews, when the Egyptians were drowned (Worthington) in the Red Sea. (Menochius)

Course. This description of the decree, or angel of the Lord, is most magnificent. The Church applies it to Christ's nativity, who is thought to have been born at midnight. (Calmet) --- It insinuated his coming, when the world should enjoy a profound peace, though buried in the darkness of ignorance. (Worthington)
Visions. These informed the Egyptians, that their miseries were not to be attributed to any natural cause. The dying proclaimed the same, as Moses had done, Exodus xi. 4.
Living. Whom the angel was prevented from attacking, Numbers xvi. 47. (Calmet)

Priestly. Literally, robe of the poderis, (Haydock) "reaching down to the feet," and made of sky-blue linen, with pomegranates and bells at the bottom.
