Afraid. Or shewed a regard for them. (Haydock) --- Great is the power of a saint, of holy vestments, and of prayer. (Menochius) --- Enough. God did not intend to exterminate his people, as he had done the first-born of Egypt. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For the saints of God there was the greatest light, when they were illuminated both outwardly by bodily light and inwardly by spiritual radiance; for the faith of God and the purity of conscience enlightened them within, whose voices the enemies heard, but whose appearance they did not see, because darkness blinded their eyes, and because, by the temptation of the plagues which came upon the Egyptians, these were not struck, but were led by heavenly guidance through the pillar of fire at night and the pillar of cloud by day, and gave worthy thanks to their Creator. Therefore, since those holy fathers who lived under the Old Testament bore the type of the saints who serve Christ under the New Testament; those in historical Egypt labored afflicted under Pharaoh, while the persecution of the Devil in the world burdens these with tribulations; for the greatest light shines for those who diligently carry the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world, in the dwelling of their heart. Indeed, the enemies hear the voice of their preaching, but do not recognize the form of the truth that is in them, and therefore do not believe them. Both the pillar of fire at night and the pillar of cloud by day lead them, because the incarnation of Christ always protects them with the shield of His protection in adversity and prosperity.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

By the merit of Egypt, they endured the punishments of darkness, who, blinded by the obscurity of envy, wished to keep the people of God, to whom the light of the divine law was to be handed down, in their prison, and although they intended not even to spare their infants, by the judgment of God, when one son, that is, Moses, was rescued from death by water, a multitude of adversaries was drowned in mighty water through his ministry. In the same way, now the spiritual enemies who strive to destroy the assembly of the faithful, when the elect of God are freed from their enemies through the water of baptism, only those enemies, together with their king the Devil, are overwhelmed in those very waters by the power of Christ. The reason for this mystery was both foreshadowed long ago in the deeds of the ancients, and is now fulfilled through the coming of Christ.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

At the time when the people of God were to be led out of Egypt by Moses and Aaron, the people themselves, still situated in Egypt, were sacrificing the Passover victim at the Lord's command; and therefore it is said that they sacrificed secretly, because, terrified by fear of their enemies, they did this in hiding, just as they learned from Moses' teaching how the law of the Passover was to be observed thereafter, having suffered the temptation of the wicked for a time, but soon to be freed from the hands of their enemies by divine help. In a similar way, even now in the times of grace, the servants of God to whom the divine law has been given for the harmony of the two Testaments, although they may be hindered for a time by their persecutors from openly celebrating the worship of the Christian religion, nevertheless cannot in any way be prevented from offering sacrifices worthy of the divine presence in the hidden places of their hearts, because it is written: The sacrifice to God is a repentant spirit; a repentant and humbled heart God does not despise (Ps. 51:17). And the same Prophet also says: In me are your vows, O God, which I will repay with praises to you (Ps. 56:12). The vows of the righteous are pleasing to the Lord, and the sacrifices of the wicked are abominable.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

It commemorates what the Book of Exodus recounts about the killing of the firstborn, when the Lord struck in the middle of the night every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in the prison, and every firstborn of the animals (Ex. 11). There, unlike before when they pretended not to agree to the departure of the Israelites, they openly urged the people of God to leave the land of Egypt quickly, saying: We shall all die.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

The Word was with God, and the Word was God (Jn. 1:1), through whom all things were made, who elsewhere is also called the arm of the Lord, as Isaiah says: And to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? (Isa. 53:1) The same is also called the right hand of the Lord because of the effective power of divine might. Therefore, the Word himself is to be understood as then executing judgment on the firstborn of the Egyptians through the ministry of the Gospel, who afterwards will sanctify for himself the firstborn of the Israelites, and now through the water of his baptism saves the multitude of believers, where he also destroyed the innumerable army of spiritual enemies. For it is said that the Lord's command carried a sharp sword; because the Word of the Lord is living and effective and more penetrating than any two-edged sword. In truth and without any deception, he judges and arranges all things; standing on earth, he reaches up to the heavens: for although incarnate he lived among men on earth, yet by his majesty he transcended all the heavenly realms.
Against Marivadus the Arian, PL 62

On the common omnipotence of the Trinity. Omnipotent Father, omnipotent Son, omnipotent Holy Spirit (2 Cor. 3:17). Concerning the Father in Solomon: your all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from the royal thrones, came (Wis. 18:15).
Against Maximinus the Arian, PL 58 5.0760A-0760B

That the Son is omnipotent is therefore taught. In Solomon it is written: Your omnipotent word, Lord, leaped from your royal throne into the midst of the doomed land (Wis. 18:15). Therefore, he is also king who holds royal thrones. Likewise in the Apocalypse: Therefore says the Son of God, who is and who was the omnipotent God. (Rev. 1:8) In the Gospel: Whatever things the Father does, these the Son does likewise (Jn. 5:19). Likewise in the Gospel: As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. In Ezekiel the Son says: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over you and those who plundered you shall be plundered, and you shall know that I am the Lord Almighty, and that the Lord Almighty is he who sent me. (Ezek. 25:7)
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

In the middle of the night, he says that the almighty God sends a word from heaven, from royal seats, a harsh conqueror, to leap into the midst of the land of destruction, and to exercise the judgment of death powerfully upon the wicked. For what is the word of the Lord, if not the Son of God? Of whom John says: In the beginning was the Word, and it is rightly said that the visions of evil dreams and unexpected fears disturbed the enemies of the people of God, so that neither to those awake nor to those sleeping was any rest given, who, because of their crimes, were destined for perpetual torments. But the very plagues warned the guilty so that they might recognize why they suffered evils, lest they perish in ignorance; this is the goodness of God, who therefore chastises sinners so that they may restrain themselves from sins and repent of past evils; but if they persist in evil and abuse the patience of God for the increase of their crimes, condemned by the just judgment of God, they will be punished without excuse in the future.
Epistle 77.4 CSEL 34

For we accuse you of nothing except the crime of schism, which by persisting wrongly you have also made into heresy. But how greatly this crime is weighed by divine judgment, read what I do not doubt you have read. You will find Dathan and Abiram swallowed up by the opening of the earth, and all the others who agreed with them consumed by fire that came out from among them. Therefore, the Lord God marked out that crime with present punishment as an example to be avoided, so that, since He now most patiently spares such people, He might show what kind of final judgment He reserves for them.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Here is recalled the story, which is narrated in the Book of Numbers, of how after the killing of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, the sons of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: You have killed the people of God. And when the sedition arose and the chaos increased, Moses and Aaron fled into the tabernacle of the covenant. And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Depart from the midst of this congregation, and I will destroy them at once. And they fell on their faces. And while they lay on the ground, Moses said to Aaron: Take the censer, and having taken fire from the altar, put incense upon it, and go quickly to the people to pray for them, for already wrath has gone out from the Lord, and the plague is raging. When Aaron had done this, and had run into the midst of the crowd, which the fire was devastating, he offered incense, and standing between the dead and the living, he prayed for the people, and the plague ceased. The number of those who were struck was fourteen thousand seven hundred, apart from those who perished in the sedition of Korah (Num. 16). From this, it must be considered how in Sodom, when at least ten were required, by whom perhaps those who dwelled in the Pentapolis of Sodom might possibly be saved, now even if only two such as Moses and Aaron are found, they can serve for the salvation of the whole nation of Israel. What then shall we say is greater in these two, what power, what merit, by which six hundred thousand and more are freed from the destruction of the destroyer? I believe that in Moses the law is signified, which teaches men the knowledge and love of God. In Aaron consists the form of appealing God and begging Him. Therefore, if it ever happens that God is angry with us or with the whole people, and the sentence of vengeance proceeds from God, but the law of God returns to our hearts, reminding us and teaching us to turn to repentance, to make satisfaction for our sins, to plead for our faults, then anger will immediately cease, anger will be calmed, the Lord will be appeased, as if Moses and Aaron were interceding for us and the whole people were petitioning. But if ever the anger of God arises and severe correction comes for sins, and our hearts are not hardened so that we do not turn to God, nor humble ourselves in His sight, so that in the confession of prayers we may lessen His wrath and anger, but on the contrary we say: God does not care about the life of mortals, nor do these things pertain to God; He has long since abandoned us, nor do these things come to His knowledge. If we think such things in our hearts, and these proceed from our mouths, it is certain that Moses and Aaron are not in us, namely the knowledge of the law and the fruits of repentance, by which we can escape the destruction of imminent ruin.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

In what he says about the robe of the ephod, which the high priest wore, that it contains the whole world, and the great deeds of the ancestors engraved on the four rows of stones, and the magnificence of God in the crown which the high priest himself wore on his head, although these express the series of all virtues which the priest of God ought to have in his teaching and conduct, nevertheless, the meaning which the Hebrews characteristic to the priestly garment, placing here its mystical significance, we reserve for discussion elsewhere. Therefore, the four colors refer to the four elements from which all things subsist: they assign linen to earth, because it is produced from the earth; purple to the sea, because it is dyed from its shellfish; blue to air, because of the similarity of color; scarlet to fire and ether, which in Hebrew is called sani; and they recall that it is just that the high priest of the Creator should pray not only for Israel, but also for the whole world. Indeed, this world consists of earth, water, air, and fire, and these elements belong to all things. Therefore, the first linen garment signifies the earth; the second, the blue one, shows the color of air, because from earthly things we are gradually lifted to the heights, and the blue robe itself, coming from the head down to the ankles, indicates the air stretched from the heavens down to the earth. The pomegranates and bells placed at the lower parts represent lightning and thunder, or earth and water, and the harmony of all the elements among themselves, and therefore all things are so intertwined that everything can be found in each part. As for the aforementioned colors being interwoven with gold, they wish it to be understood that the vital color and the providence of divine sense penetrate all things. Over the ephod and the two stones, either emerald or onyx, which are above and cover each shoulder, they interpret as two hemispheres, one above the earth, the other below, or as the sun and moon which shine above. That belt by which the priest's chest is tightened, and the linen tunic, that is, the earth, is bound, they interpret as the ocean. The breastplate placed in the middle they explain as the earth, which, like a point, although it contains all things in itself, is nevertheless surrounded by all the elements. The twelve stones are interpreted as the circle of the zodiac, or the twelve months, and to each verse is assigned a particular time, and to these are given three months each. Fittingly, this very thing in the middle is called the breastplate of judgment; for all things are full of reason, and earthly things are connected to heavenly things. The intermingling of earthly things and the times of heat and cold, and the double temperance between each, descends from the course and order of the heavens, therefore also the breastplate is more tightly bound with the ephod. Furthermore, what is said in the breastplate, "and analogy," that is, indicator and teaching or truth, signifies that there is never any falsehood in the reason of God, but that truth itself is shown to men by many signs and arguments, and comes even to mortals. Therefore it has come about that we know the course of the sun and moon, and of the year, and of the months, and of the times, and of the hours, and also of the sowing seasons and winds and all things, receiving the wisdom implanted by God, and with God himself, the inhabitant and teacher of his own dwelling, showing us also the knowledge of the structure; above all, the mitre and the blue ribbon represent the heavens, and the plate of gold which is on the forehead of the high priest, and the name of God written on it, show that all things below are governed by the will of God.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 2:3.6

The name "world" is often used in the Scriptures with different meanings. What in Latin we call "world," the Greeks call kosmos, and kosmos not only means "world" but also "ornament." In fact, in Isaiah, when a reproach is made against the powerful children of Zion, it is said, "Instead of golden ornaments you will be bald, because of your works," where "ornament" is indicated with the word that means "world," that is, kosmos. And it is also said that the explanation of the world was contained in the pontifical vestment, as we find in the Wisdom of Solomon, where it says, "The entire world was in the priestly vestment." Our earth with its inhabitants is also called world, as when the Scripture says that "the whole world is in the possession of the evil one." And Clement, disciple of the apostles, refers to those places that the Greeks called antipodes and to the other parts of the earth where no one can reach (just as none of the people there can reach us), and he calls them "world," saying, "The ocean cannot be crossed by people, nor the worlds that are beyond them, which are governed by the very dispositions of the Lord God." We also call world this universe that is formed by the heavens and the earth, as Paul says, "The form of this world is passing away." And our Lord and Savior also speaks of another beyond this visible world, which is difficult to describe and define in its reality. He says, "I do not come from this world." As though he came from another world, he said, "I do not come from this world." We said that it is difficult to describe this world, so as to not provide anyone with occasion to claim that we assert the existence of the images that the Greeks call ideas. In fact, it is foreign to our way of thinking to assert the existence of an incorporeal world, consisting solely in the fantasy of the mind and fallacious thoughts.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, the devastator who was sent feared the spiritual, not the figurative, appearance, because he recognized the greatness of the true Pontiff. Now ascend to the higher traces of this word, and from there see how the true Pontiff, Jesus Christ, having assumed the staff of human flesh and placed upon it the fire of the altar, with the soul undoubtedly that magnificent one with which he was born in the flesh, and also adding incense, which is the immaculate spirit standing between the living and the dead, stood, and did not allow death to spread further, but as the Apostle says: He destroyed him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil, so that whoever believes in him may no longer die, but live forever (Heb. 2:14-15). This, therefore, was the mystery that the one who was devastating the people already feared would happen later; for he recognized the figure of the staff and the fire and the incense and what kind of offering should be made to God by him who stood between the dead and the living, he foresaw. And indeed, at that time the prefigured image saved them; but for us, the truth of salvation itself has arrived, nor would that devastator angel have been ashamed of the pontiff's garments woven of purple, wool, and linen.

n: Knew. God foresaw the malice of the Egyptians against his people, but as not the author of it. (Worthington)
Care. Literally, "solicitude," (Haydock) so that they would not allow them time to prepare victuals.
Necessity. God permitted them to be blinded by their own obstinacy. (Calmet) --- They rushed headlong into the channel of the Red Sea. (Haydock)
Beginning. It seemed susceptible of any form; and the elements appeared to be of another nature. The fire burnt in water, the sea retired, &c., chap. v. 21., and xvi. 24.

Field. Like a meadow, (Calmet) germinans, "growing grass." (Septuagint) (Haydock) --- Pliny ([Natural History?] xiii. 25.) attests, that "the Red Sea, and all the eastern ocean, are full of wood." The Hebrews passed with as much ease as in a desert, (Psalm cv. 9., and Isaias lxiii. 13.) or place of pasture, while the sea seemed to be in quest of other channels. (Calmet) (Genesis i. 9.) (Haydock)
Thunders. Which took place at the destruction of Sodom, for their warning. (Calmet)

In another. Literally, "but there was another respect (or punishment) of them, because unwillingly they received strangers," Genesis xix. 1. (Haydock) --- The Amorrhites would not admit the Israelites, Numbers xxi. 21. (Worthington)
Laws. Or "rights," justitiis. The Hebrews acknowledged the civil authority (Menochius) of Pharao, though they adopted not his religion, chap. xviii. 4. (Haydock)

Changed. The meaning is, that whatever changes God wrought in the elements by miracles in favour of his people, they still kept their harmony by obeying his will. (Challoner) --- He answers the objection of philosophers, who argued against the possibility of miracles, as being against the established laws of nature. But they induce no more confusion than the various strings of a harp, when they are touched with skill, though they have each their respective name and sound. The ancients frequently compared the harmony of the universe to a musical instrument. See plut.[Plutarch?] Macrobius, som. ii. --- Sight. Septuagint add, "of what happened" (Haydock) in those miraculous changes.
Water. Men, &c., passed through the Red Sea, while frogs got into houses.

Therein. For the punishment of the Egyptians, chap. xvi. 18. (Calmet) --- Food. Manna. (Challoner) --- Septuagint, "immortal food," ambrosia. (Haydock) --- Place. This conclusion agrees very well with the preceding observations. But it seems some thing should be said respecting the original petition for wisdom; whence we conclude, with Grotius, that the work is imperfect: (Calmet) though this is by no means clear, as the prayer is sufficiently expressed in the nine first chapters, if not in the whole book, and God answers it, 3 Kings ix. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For this reason, vengeance came upon the enemies of the people of God until the end, because in their morals and life there was no worthy amendment. Therefore, with pretended arguments they pretend repentance, and for this reason, from the inspector of hearts, they did not receive perfect forgiveness. Therefore it is read in Exodus that Pharaoh, when any plague was divinely inflicted upon him and his people, immediately promised to let the people of God go if he escaped the present danger, but after a short interval, he returned again to his former cruelty, until at last, when he was pursuing the departing people, he was drowned and perished in the waves of the Red Sea (Ex. 14). Such is indeed the stubbornness of the unbelieving and proud enemies of the name of Christ, that when they persist hopelessly in wickedness, they finally feel by experience how great is the justice of the omnipotent God in judging.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Every creature from the beginning is restored to its own kind when it obeys the commands of its Creator and serves His will in all things. For this is the purpose of creation: that it might become subject and obedient to its Creator. How the cloud covered the camp of the Israelites, shining for them at night and shading them against the heat of the sun by day, and how the Red Sea, divided, prepared a way for the people of God and, when it returned upon itself, drowned their enemies, is clearly explained in the history of Exodus. Nor is it any less clear that the cloud which led the people of God signifies the incarnation of Christ, who enlightens believers in this world with the light of the Gospel and protects and guards them by His grace from their persecutors. The Red Sea, moreover, bears the ritual of baptism, where the faithful are saved and the opposing powers are drowned; just as then the children of Israel, having been delivered, sang praises to the Lord, rejoicing with great exultation.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Therefore, we also ought at all times to give thanks to our Creator for our deliverance, exulting and saying with the Prophet: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits (Ps. 103:2). The Apostle also seems to teach us this, saying: Pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you (1 Thess. 5:16-18).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Note, wise reader, that for the adversaries of God the earth produced flies, and the river brought forth frogs; but for the worshippers of God the earth gave fruit and the sea provided meat as food, because it is fitting that through His works divine providence should acquire nourishment for His faithful. For His enemies, however, it is fitting that through the creatures subject to Him, the justice of the Almighty should prepare appropriate torment.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For if those who harshly and mercilessly treated the ancient servants of God, who came to them out of profane necessity, received fitting punishments, so that, darkened in mind and hardened in feeling, they endured the obscurity of darkness and various idols in bodily sense, how much more will those who dishonorably reject and despise the servants of Christ and preachers of the Gospel be eternally tormented with immeasurable and unspeakable punishments. Therefore, Truth itself says to the disciples: Whoever does not receive you or listen to your words, as you go out from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Truly, I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city (Matt. 10:14-15). And it is rightly said that they were struck with blindness, just as those were blinded by darkness who wandered at the doors of the righteous man, that is, Lot, seeking the entrance to his door and not finding it; for whoever suffers the darkness of error within is hemmed in on all sides by the gravest losses, since he has not known the way of life. And that door of which the Gospel says, I am the door; if anyone enters by me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture, the one who wanders will not be able to find it (Jn. 10:9).
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

Just as in the instrument of the organ, different sounds differ from each other, but musicians agree to temper them for the harmony of the melody, so also, although the various elements differ from each other in quality, they are nevertheless bent to the will of their Creator, preserving the law of their nature; for our Maker did not create His creation contrary to Himself, but made it in all things conformable to His will.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

For men and beasts crossed the depths of the Red Sea on dry ground, and frogs coming out of the rivers filled the houses of the Egyptians. Fire mixed with hail rained down from heaven, and neither did fire shun water, nor water shun fire, but falling together, they struck the land of the Egyptians. But where the children of Israel were, they harmed no one, so as to show that all the elements of the world not only strive for their own nature, but are subject and serve the will of their Creator.
Commentary on Wisdom, PL 109

This closing passage of the book makes mention not only of the faithful of former Fathers, but also of those present and future at the same time, because our virtuous and merciful Creator, almighty God, never abandons nor will abandon those who hope in Him; rather, He cherishes, protects, and governs them with caring help. Nor should anyone object to us that the bodies of the holy martyrs are handed over into the hands of their persecutors, because this is permitted not for their condemnation, but for their testing, so that just as gold in the furnace of fire is not destroyed but tested, so too the souls of the elect, examined by the fire of tribulation, may be rendered more precious in the sight of their Creator. For it is written: The furnace tests the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests just men (Sirach 27:5). For many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken. He will redeem the souls of His servants, and none of those who hope in Him will be forsaken (Ps. 34:22).

intro: THE BOOK OF WISDOM. INTRODUCTION. This book is so called, because it treats of the excellence of Wisdom, the means to obtain it, and the happy fruits it produces. It is written in the person of Solomon, and contains his sentiments. But it is uncertain who was the writer. It abounds with instructions and exhortations to kings and magistrates to administer justice in the commonwealth, teaching all kinds of virtues under the general names of justice and wisdom. It contains also many prophecies of Christ's coming, passion, resurrection, and other Christian mysteries. The whole may be divided into three parts: [1.] In the six first chapters, the author admonishes all superiors to love and exercise justice and wisdom. [2.] In the next three, he teacheth that wisdom proceedeth only from God, and is procured by prayer, and a good life. [3.] In the other ten chapters, he sheweth the excellent effects, and utility of wisdom and justice. (Challoner) --- Their authority is surely greater than that of the Jews, (Calmet) whom Protestants choose to follow. (Haydock) --- Before they attack us, they must, however, answer this prescription. (Calmet) --- St. Irenæus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, St. Athanasius, &c., attribute this book to Solomon; and, though St. Jerome and St. Augustine call this in question, they maintain its divine authority. Sometimes the Fathers abstain from urging it against the Jews, because they[the Jews] reject it, for the same reason as our Saviour proved the immortality of the soul, against the Sadducees, from the books of Moses alone, though other texts might have been adduced. The Councils of Carthage, 419, Florence, Trent, &c., declare this book canonical, (Worthington) agreeably to the ancient Fathers. (St. Augustine, Præd. xiv., and City of God xvii. 20., &c.) --- Philo (St. Jerome) the elder, (Worthington; Menochius) one of the Septuagint (Genebrard) might compile this work from the sentences of Solomon, preserved by tradition, as Sirach's son did that of Ecclesiasticus; (Worthington) or it is styled "Solomon's Wisdom," (Septuagint; Haydock) on account of its resembling his works, in like manner as the Second of Kings is called Samuel's, though he wrote none of that book. (Worthington) --- Sixtus (Bib. viii. hær. ix.) and others, maintain, that this was written originally in Hebrew, and some think by Solomon; being translated by the Septuagint. But these go too far. (Calmet) --- The nine first chapters seem, however, to be the production of Solomon, though the latter may have been added by the Greek translator, (Houbigant) who must, therefore, have been divinely inspired. (Haydock) --- The sentiments are very grand, (Calmet) and contain a prediction of the sufferings of the just one, whence we may infer, that the name of the author was originally in the title, like that of all other prophets. The arguments which Calmet adduces, to prove that Solomon was not the author of the first part of this work, may easily be refuted. In the New Testament, that part is frequently quoted, whence we may gather, that it was allowed to be the work of Solomon. (Houbigant, præf. p. 176.) --- Some style this work Panaretos, as being an exhortation to all virtues. (Calmet) --- All the five sapiential books (Proverbs, &c.) are cited under the title of Wisdom in the mass-book. Superiors are here admonished to act with justice, and taught that wisdom is to be obtained by prayer, and by a good life, chap. ix. Its effect and utility (Worthington) form the subject of the latter part. See Apocrypha, vol. i. p. 597. (Haydock)
